This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for approximating functions governed by the time-independent Schrödinger equation. We establish that a finite network can achieve a network function $\mathcal{N}_\mu$ that can approximate the ground state and excited states, along with their eigenvalues, with specified accuracy. We also demonstrate that the ground state function, together with its eigenvalue, has the property of belonging to a specific type of two-dimensional spectral space known as the spectral Barron space. We establish an upper limit for the spectral complexity of a neural network representing the ground state, which scales logarithmically with respect to the spectral radius of the potential function. We establish lower and upper bounds on the ground state functions for a particular type of potential function. We further develop a new theory on the spectral space and demonstrate that a neural network's activation functions can be parameter-free after training, reducing the problem to a matter of selecting the right initial parameters for the network. We also formulate an optimization problem for minimalizing a specific loss function that is parameter-free for the spectral space, which corresponds to a two-layer neural network for solving the time-independent Schrödinger equation. We run experiments on the hydrogen atom, the helium atom, and some complicated models. We demonstrate that a small spectral complexity can produce accurate energy eigenvalues for the model, which suggests a necessary condition for efficient generalization performance in solving the time-independent Schrödinger equation.

Our in-depth study of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory has revealed a significant anisotropy pattern. In addition to a 20% anisotropy amplitude observed at energies above 30 EeV, a stronger 27% amplitude is found at energies between 6 and 8 EeV. This earlier analysis indicated an energy-dependent increase in anisotropy, but the current results reveal a local dip at energies around 6-8 EeV. This unusual behavior may offer a crucial clue about the origin of these extremely energetic particles.

Homogenization outcomes for thin films, reduced by dimensional reduction, were derived 
under periodic or almost periodic hypotheses in film mid-plane energies. In this note, 
we discuss thin films, resulting from cross-sections of periodic mediums, with incommensurate 
mid-planes - containing no period other than zero - and demonstrate a generalized 
homogenization outcome via geometric, almost periodic reasoning.

We establish the existence of long-term solutions, starting with minimal initial conditions, for a semilinear equation governing the behavior of half-spin particles within a Lorentz group framework. Our findings expand upon the work of F. Lochak and B. Majorana, showing that a solution will consistently exist for any initial condition within a certain margin of measure. We derive an accurate estimate of the maximum value of the initial condition required for the solution's existence, which depends on a parameter $\lambda$ in the equation. As the parameter $\lambda$ increases without bound, our solution aligns with the original result obtained by Lochak and Majorana, but for smaller values of $\lambda$, our solution provides a notable expansion of their work.

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification task with two categories. By collaborating with seven expert histology institutions, we assembled a large and diverse dataset containing a total of 29,300 digitized tissue sections. Our results showed that models trained using federated learning using different methods, such as PyMoFL, FedAvg, and a custom implementation, demonstrated improved generalizability compared to models trained on a single institution's data. Furthermore, our model trained via federated learning with the most advanced method, adapted from Adam, generalised well across the range of digitized tissue sections from our partner institutions.

Cavity magnomechanics provides a unique setting for exploring the macroscopic quantum effects by merging magnons and phonons.  Cavity magnomechanics has an advantageous characteristic that enables non-linear phonon-magnon interactions, which are essential for various quantum transformations.  To improve the efficiency of a phonon-upconversion protocol, researchers have recently introduced a new Cavity magnomechanical setup, which utilizes a post-processing technique to simplify and analyze the system's behavior through a quantum stochastic master equation approach.  The system's ability to up-convert phonons into magnons and then into photons is demonstrated through simulations, which also investigate the influence of several technical limitations.  Furthermore, the team has discovered an innovative method for generating non-classical states with enhanced squeezing, which is achieved by leveraging the non-classical characteristics of the phonon field.

Recently, a major advancement in quadrupedal locomotion control has been achieved through the application of Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, most research relies on complex, physics-based simulators that require considerable computational resources for RL training, and their generalizability through domain adaptation from simulation to reality remains a pressing concern. A novel approach is presented in this paper, leveraging RL with an evolved metric space for trajectory generation to develop a generalizable quadrupedal locomotion controller. By employing an Evolutionary Strategy (ES) to create diverse foot trajectories and transform them into Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) for real-time optimization, this method achieves real-time model-predictive-like planning without requiring a precise dynamical model. Furthermore, the proposed RL structure facilitates generalization by transforming planning information about the terrain into a novel input feature. By training the policy in a simple MFC-Gym environment with a synthetic terrain and applying it to a MuJoCS-based simulation with diverse terrain types, our approach successfully demonstrates successful adaptation to various challenging scenarios through four key factors: the inclusion of a planning frequency in the state space, the absence of a predefined gait in trajectory generation, the application of CBF constraints for safer navigation, and the application of the policy to a physical Titan robot on diverse real-world terrains.

A significant number of galaxies host a central super-massive black hole (SMBH), and a variety of observations have established a strong link between these objects. Observing the activities of low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) poses a significant challenge, and their impact on the evolution of the galaxies they reside in may be even more significant. This study presents a novel approach for identifying LLAGNs within a sample of 3155 X-ray selected galaxies using a random forest classifier and an extensive dataset from the SDSS and MPA/JLA catalog. Our results indicate that a substantial 55% of the galaxies in the sample are classified as LLAGNs, and their characteristics are analyzed in terms of their redshift, stellar mass, and other properties. A comparison with the results of LLAGN identification from the LLAGN hunt project is conducted, and a reasonable level of agreement is found. A correlation is found between LLAGN fraction and galaxy density in the L* bulge surface density, and this correlation is compared with existing literature on LLAGNs and their impact on the evolution of the universe.

Closed-loop system performance can be enhanced through reinforcement learning (RL)-based controller redesign by directly mapping states to actions through trial and error.  However, this approach demands numerous interactions with the system, posing challenges for controller design, especially when implemented on high-power systems that cannot be tested through multiple RL iterations.  Utilizing a pre-trained reward function from offline data and online interaction in an iterative process significantly reduces numerous System Input-Output responses necessary for parameter convergence.  Furthermore, it minimizes the need for numerous system inputs and Output (IO) responses typically required in online Model Predictive Control (MPC) models.  Furthermore, it minimizes the number of IO typically required in online MPC models.  In this investigation, a novel iterative algorithm is proposed that iteratively refines model parameters by incorporating the e-Kalman Filter and the Iterative Dynamic Programming method.  Using a pre-trained action-value function derived from offline data to approximate the current cost function's gradient, the algorithm enables faster convergence and fewer IO exchanges.  Several case studies were conducted in simulation involving a nonlinear, multi-input multi-output system with time-varying delays, and compared the convergence rate and accuracy of the proposed algorithm with Kalman Filter-based MPC and standard MPC methods.  Results showed an 80% reduction in IO exchanges and a 10% improvement in convergence accuracy.

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, designed with a sophisticated design to achieve high accuracy in measuring the momentum and mass of particles. Its streamlined interior, clear view of interaction point, and position of tracking, calorimetry, and muon systems contribute to its excellent resolution. In a simplified model of an electron orbiting within the SiD detector, we'll examine how the detector system breaks the symmetry, with the tracking system breaking rotational symmetry and the solenoid magnetic field breaking Lorentz invariance.

We have obtained high-resolution spectra for 109 red giant stars in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. With effective temperatures below 4800 K and metallicities ranging between $-2.05 < [Fe/H] < -1.95$, these giant stars allow us to accurately study the composition of this cluster. Our analysis reveals that nearly the entire dataset exhibits an [N/O] ratio exceeding solar levels. Given Tononzintla 2's negligible young star content, we interpret the nitrogen enrichment as a sign of early first-generation star activity within the cluster. Given its low star formation fraction $f_{\rm{4He}} = 0.12 \pm 0.03$, Tononzintla 2 serves as a representative example of the majority of metal-poor cluster populations.

Remote sensing, specifically through Earth observation, enables comprehensive monitoring and analysis of the environment and specific targets by utilizing various datasets such as radar, thermal, and optical imagery, as well as hyperspectral and multispectral data. This process is crucial for numerous applications, including agriculture, wildlife monitoring, climate change monitoring, and disaster monitoring and management. These applications necessitate the continuous and real-time detection of target objects and anomalies. Machine and deep learning methods have significantly enhanced object detection and anomaly detection capabilities in Earth observation datasets. This review provides an in-depth analysis of recent advancements in these areas, covering data representation, machine learning, and deep learning techniques, as well as real-world applications. The challenges and future prospects for object detection and anomaly detection in remote sensing are also discussed in relation to their various applications.

A step-by-step construction of a general active nematic frame in two dimensions
is developed, which is crucial for reducing complex, nonlinear equations to a
manageable form. This framework is then applied to a flow decomposition method
that produces a closed set of equations with a particular nonlinearity that does not
significantly affect its behavior. Consequently, a stable solution exists for the
rotation of a stick, which serves as a useful example to illustrate a broader range
of effects in active nematics. Furthermore, the method's potential to be applied to
other research areas, such as the interaction between an active nematic and a flow
induced by a rotating object, is highlighted.

Identifying irregularities in urban data is a pressing issue, given the vast amount of sensor data being generated by the increasing number of city dwellers, all of which are now being monitored through various technologies such as sensors, cameras, and GPS devices. Existing methods for detecting irregularities typically require detailed information about specific areas and local expertise to define what constitutes normal patterns, which is often impractical and time-consuming. We introduce an innovative approach for automatically detecting irregularities in large datasets without the need for prior knowledge. Our technique utilizes the information from each data point and how it interacts with its neighbors in space and over time to establish a baseline of typical behavior. We then compare this to actual data to spot deviations that could be considered irregularities. We applied this method to spot irregularities in traffic data at a junction in Manhattan, and successfully identified several notable events, such as the impact of Hurricane Sandy, the closure of Manhattan Bridge, and incidents involving major road closures and data anomalies.

This study examines the $e^+e^-$ annihilation process into meson pairs via the intermediate state of the omega ($\omega$) meson. Utilizing the Fluctuation Dissipation Theorem, a relationship is established between the branching fraction of the reaction $\omega \to \pi\pi$ and experimentally measurable data. By analyzing the phase shift of $p$-wave $\pi\pi$ scattering at the energy of the omega resonance and electronic data near this energy, the study derives a constraint on the branching fraction. As a result, the study finds that $Br(\omega \to \pi\pi) < 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$ with a confidence level of 95%.

This paper presents GraphCodeOne, an large language model trained on graphs representing code, which enables it to capture code's structure, semantics, and dependencies. By establishing this novel model, we found GraphCodeOne to be superior in tasks like code segment matching, far outperforming previous state-of-the-art models, and also excelling in more complex code understanding tasks. We define code embeddings as node representations in these graphs and use them to train a model that predicts aggregated, meaningful graph node features from individual code tokens. GraphCodeOne's success stems from its ability to learn code's inherent hierarchical structure and leverage node representations to capture code's complex characteristics. We developed this model by creating GraphCodeOne from code graphs and employing a innovative training strategy that uses node features to capture code's characteristics.

The relation between a galaxy's mass in stars and its surrounding dark matter halo mass has been established for early-type galaxies by analyzing their near-infrared luminosity and holographic properties from the GW17501 dataset of 17 early-type galaxies. By employing a novel selection method, it was possible to gather data for galaxies with a range of masses, from those with a mass a ten times lower to those with a mass ten times higher than the median mass. We found that early-type galaxies' peak mass in stars occurs at the median mass, but those with masses significantly above or below the peak exhibit mass relations that diverge from the peak, with less stellar mass per unit of dark matter in both cases. These findings align with those in earlier, more comprehensive studies of SHMR, but our new data provide crucial constraints for models of SHMR, especially for galaxies with low masses, which had not been adequately constrained before.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere is a straightforward approach, its precision is limited to about 10% in absolute terms, making it challenging to reach high-precision measurements required to detect subtle climate variations. By taking multiple photographs of the same airglow layer at different times, we can significantly enhance precision to as low as 0.1% at a confidence level of one sigma. Nevertheless, achieving such high precision demands a substantial number of photographs, around 50, to account for potential measurement errors. Our research successfully demonstrated a 30-fold increase in precision using images from the ZENITH instrument on the CALTECH 1.5m telescope, detecting a 30-milliarcsecond shift and a corresponding 0.003 change in optical depth. Although obtaining such a large number of images may not be feasible with current ZENITH data, new technology like the LSST could collect up to 600 images in a single night, paving the way for detecting extremely subtle atmospheric optical shifts and associated climate variations.

We modify the Graphical Lasso approach by incorporating a penalty that differentiates between inclusion and exclusion of terms, allowing for non-symmetric variable selection. The proposed method outperforms existing techniques in promoting sparse precision matrices and demonstrates superior accuracy in predicting target variables. The new penalty surpasses traditional methods by providing more accurate results when selecting variables.

Using the ALMA for a second time, we've obtained higher-resolution and sensitivity data of the TW Hydrae system, which allows us to dissect its emission into distinct components: a disc, photoevaporative tail, and possible corona. At a resolution of 11 AU, we detect millimeter-wave emission from the disc extending up to 160 AU, which aligns with the visual emission's outer limit of 130 AU, as well as the disc's surface profile. A newly developed method employs IRF deconvolution to dissect low-resolution images into intrinsic components, which we've applied to analyse disc emission up to 11 AU. Using this technique, we detect millimeter-wave emission from the TW Hydrae disc extending up to 160 AU, which reveals a power law slope of 2.96 \pm 0.08, which becomes shallower at larger radii, which may be attributed to a less opaque size distribution or a disc inclined at 42.6 degrees. Photoevaporation appears to dominate the emission at 1.3 mm, which constitutes about 80% of the total emission, which shows a distinct break at 230 AU. The remaining 20% of the total emission is likely contributed by the corona. By applying a simple model, we estimate a mass-loss rate of 10^-13 g/s, which is comparable to the values obtained from X-ray-driven

For speech processing applications, tasks such as speech voicing, fundamental frequency estimation, and dynamic pitch tracking are essential components that require efficient algorithms to be successfully implemented. This algorithmic suite is designed to address voicing detection with the goal of distinguishing between voiced and unvoiced speech segments accurately. A proposed technique achieves this objective by leveraging a hybrid approach that combines time and frequency analysis. This approach aims to adapt to the specific voice characteristics of individual speakers while automating the process as much as possible. The results of this study showcase a significant improvement in accuracy, reaching a recognition rate of 98.3% on a diverse set of speech samples from various speakers. This research also extends to a general-purpose voice activity detection system that operates within a limited computational framework, making it suitable for real-time processing on resource-constrained devices like mobile phones. A voice activity detector is developed with the objective of pinpointing precise speech boundaries within an environment that may contain background noise. This system involves two key stages: initial speech detection and refinement of speech boundaries. A fundamental hypothesis is that a speech frame is considered active if its energy surpasses a predetermined threshold. This approach is built upon the concept of a masked spectrum derived from log-power spectral analysis. A fundamental frequency estimator and a dynamic pitch tracker are essential tools used to process speech signals and background noise within a framework of minimal computational requirements. We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle structured monotone inclusion problems. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, we develop a globally convergent solution that outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, we provide a globally convergent primal-dual version of DWIFOB and show through numerical tests that it surpasses the performance of the Chambolle-Pock algorithm and the Tikhonov regularized Anderson acceleration, while exhibiting enhanced robustness and reliability.

This research takes place within the next-to-minimal supergravity Standard Model, which incorporates two Higgs doublets and a single singlet scalar field. By eliminating a trilinear scalar term involving these fields, we prevent a CP-violating problem at the electroweak scale. Within this framework, a well-established seesaw mechanism using a Yukawa coupling between the singlet scalar and the Higgs doublets enables us to produce extremely small neutrino masses. Furthermore, we show that loop-induced couplings between these fields and Standard Model particles can drive the baryon asymmetry of the universe through mechanisms of matter generation and electroweak symmetry breaking. As a result, we are able to fit the complete set of neutrino oscillation data and also make a prediction for the lightest neutrino mass. Ultimately, we determine that a lepton number violating decay of a neutral pion into two neutrinos becomes feasible, with its detection possibility becoming an experimentally testable prediction.

The integration of neural architecture search (NAS) has significantly reduced the cost of automated architecture search in deep learning applications. Despite its success, most NAS techniques are constrained by a predefined search space, and when the search space is expanded, these methods typically fail or require substantial adjustments. To overcome this limitation, we developed a search spatial separation (SSS) framework, which separates the search space into a static component, characterizing architectural parametricity, and a dynamic component, involved in search and model training,. As a result, our framework can facilitate NAS on abstract search spaces, such as those including split ops, without the need for time-consuming pre-training. Furthermore, SSS can be combined with various static search space characterization strategies, resulting in improved performance when using our framework. To validate its efficacy, we compared the SSS framework with state-of-the-art NAS methods on an extensive search space containing approximately 20k architecture candidates. Our findings demonstrate that SSS-based methods significantly outperform traditional NAS approaches, achieving more than 1000 man-hours savings in terms of optimization iterations and showing superior accuracy on the ImageNet dataset after pruning.

The advantages of multicast beamforming in terms of reliability, low system cost, and reduced latency have led to significant interest in deploying it in wireless networks. However, due to its sensitivity to channel conditions, its potential benefit in terms of spectral efficiency is often compromised. In this context, we develop a low-complexity beamforming scheme that balances the trade-off between complexity and spectral efficiency. This scheme involves determining the optimal number of multicast groups under individual user rate constraints using the SDR method with a limited number of simultaneous transmissions. In addition, we create an algorithm for computing multicast group sizes that ensures a sufficient system support while maximizing the number of groups. Finally, we devise a simplified beamforming approach that reduces computational load without significantly compromising efficiency. Our proposed method demonstrates substantial reductions in system complexity, along with improved spectral efficiency, when compared to unicast transmission.

Federated Learning's federated distillation approach, which involves training on centralized data excerpts, is being explored as a more efficient communication method compared to traditional Federated Averaging. A new FDP3 algorithm has been developed to enhance this approach, allowing for efficient training while preserving privacy. The innovation of FDP3 lies in using personalized data excerpts tailored to local client preferences, which reduces privacy risks and improves performance. Moreover, a soft ensembling technique within these excerpts minimizes over-smoothing and delivers superior results than other methods.

A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to support future-proof services through a name-based paradigm for data exchange. This approach aligns seamlessly with decentralized computing architectures, making it an ideal networking option. Our study focuses on NDN's suitability for distributed deep learning models by assessing its network capabilities using a simulated NDN environment enhanced with network simulation. Our evaluation centered around four key metrics - latency, throughput, overhead, and packet delay loss - under two specific distributed computing applications. Our results demonstrate that NDN's distributed computing applications outperform traditional data center networks in terms of latency, overhead, and packet delay loss, but show increased latency in terms of throughput.

We tackle the challenging inverse problem of determining parameters from eigenvalues for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped metric graph with external moments applied at its vertices. The crucial first step, calculating the eigenvectors and establishing their exponential stability, is shown to lead to a significant advantage. Specifically, this enables demonstration of the uniqueness and stability of the solution. A key finding is that the direct problem's solution exists and is unique, and we derive asymptotic estimates for the direct problem, which in turn facilitate proof of the solution's stability. The rate of this stability is inversely proportional to the square root of the index of the inverse problem.

In the quark-meson model with a specific type of symmetry breaking, we investigate the influence of inhomogeneous phases on the equilibrium of the system. Our analysis reveals that the system can enter such an inhomogeneous state within certain parameter ranges, primarily with a specific wavelength. However, this phenomenon is largely confined to regions where the system does not exhibit certain properties with the standard interactions of the system. Increasing the mass of the pions within the system tends to eliminate the inhomogeneous phases, while a certain type of interaction within the system, known as the cubic interaction, is crucial for the system to achieve the lowest energy state through inhomogeneous phases.

Using a combination of experimental and computational data, we investigated the time-dependent and time-independent properties of the topological material PdPtPn (Pn = P, As). Our study reveals that the material PdPtPn undergo a band inversion between its s and p bands near the Fermi level, and this phenomenon is a result of a strong hybridization between its s and p bands. We found that this band inversion is influenced by two key factors, which are the crystal structure of PdPtPn and the presence of time-reversal symmetry. Our results demonstrate that replacing the platinum component with other heavier elements such as iridium in palladium-based compounds may lead to the emergence of topological properties in more compound systems.

In multi-objective optimization, there is often a challenge in translating expert knowledge about desired outcomes into a single utility function due to the complexities of this process. This is exacerbated by the need for extensive expert involvement, which can be time-consuming and costly. Furthermore, standard methods are generally only able to verify if the obtained solution meets the criteria, but not to identify and correct any shortcomings in the utility function. To address these issues, we introduce an iterative approach that interweaves an batch learning algorithm called Multi-Armed Bandits With Experts and an utility function manager. This collaborative system allows for a continuous refinement of the utility function based on alternating interactions. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we compare our proposed method to other state-of-the-art algorithms in a batch learning setting. Additionally, we show that the collaboration between experts and the bandit algorithm leads to a utility function that more accurately reflects the true preferences. To validate our findings, we conduct thorough experiments on various problems. Finally, a method proposed by us enables us to pinpoint any areas where the actual utility function diverges from that probed by our algorithm.

Recent findings in reinforcement learning indicate that agents learned through operant conditioning can be vulnerable to manipulation via adversarial samples. This phenomenon occurs when agents are trained to be responsive to manipulative rewards provided by an external agent, known as the trainer. Our study builds upon these findings by creating a more nuanced trainer that can not only provide initial training but also engage with the agent after training has concluded. This secondary trainer, which possesses a level of manipulative intent, can engage the target agent in a complex series of interactions that may include both positive and negative rewards, ultimately leading to the development of a more sophisticated relationship between the two.

Our investigation into a 2D electronic lattice reveals a non-trivial Dirac cone structure, differing from the established models of graphene and berkerdopfer lattices, which exhibit equivalent band dispersions. In our proposed diamond lattice model, we incorporate an additional internal orbital degree of freedom, enabling a distinct Dirac cone configuration within the same Brillouin zone. We explore the impact of orbital coupling on the band structure and demonstrate that increasing orbital interaction can isolate the Dirac cones and induce gapping, with the gaps displaying linear relationships based on the specific mode of orbital coupling.

A change in environment or model in reinforcement learning (RL) often causes risk-sensitive RL algorithms to diverge from their expected values. To address this issue, various RL methods have been developed that assume a non-stationary risk threshold. These algorithms typically require knowledge of the total allowed reward variation over time, or a point at which it changes. In many real-world RL applications, this information is not readily available. To overcome this limitation, we develop a framework for efficient risk-sensitive RL in non-stationary, partial observable environments with a known or unknown total allowed reward variation. We use a non-stochastic risk measure based on a budget in our design. Our total-variation budget model is particularly suitable for handling non-stationary problems and is superior to other common models. We employ an online ridge tracking approach to build a simple, yet effective risk-sensitive RL algorithm, which successfully tracks the optimal risk-sensitive policy over time with the least number of changes needed. We extend its use to partially observable problems by integrating it with the Particle-Filter. We demonstrate the suitability of our budget measure in non-stationary risk-sensitive RL and show through simulations that our total-variation budget model outperforms other common models.

Issue tracking systems have long been a staple in software project management, enabling teams to collaborate on enhancing product functionality and resolving problems through prioritized task lists. While computer support for project management has improved, many systems still fall short in prioritizing tasks automatically. To address this limitation, we propose an explicit and straightforward representation of task priorities along with a set of learned policies capable of predicting them based on task metadata such as release deadlines, feature types, and issue descriptions. By utilizing past Task Reports from the open-source community, our approach yields precise predictions on average, surpassing existing predictive models by a significant margin of 8-10%.

Decentralized machine learning applications are gaining popularity due to the increased demand for efficient data collection and utilization. As a result, a new paradigm of distributed machine learning has gained traction, where multiple devices collaborate to train models over dynamically changing network conditions. However, these network conditions pose significant challenges, leading to issues like bias and instability in model convergence. In response, researchers have developed algorithms that facilitate model convergence but often at the cost of significant differences in objective values compared to ideal models. In this study, we introduce two novel algorithms, average gradient descent and gradient mean square bias machine learning, that ensure linear convergence to an objective value near-optimal with a guaranteed error margin. We provide rigorous mathematical proofs for the linear convergence of these methods under time-varying network conditions. The effectiveness of these algorithms has been demonstrated through rigorous theoretical analysis and extensive numerical experiments.

A new type of optical dipole trap has been developed using a specially designed chip with multiple grating structures to capture and manipulate individual Rubidium atoms. By exploiting the diffraction effect, five focused trap points can be created, with an experimental diameter of around 5.6 micrometers. This innovative design achieves an axial inter-trap spacing of approximately 5.15 micrometers, essentially reaching the atomic diffraction limit. When a single Rb atom is loaded into the trap, an optical pumping technique is applied to facilitate Raman sideband cooling on an optical transition, and the successful cooling of the Rb atom is confirmed by detecting blue-sideband responses through a single-photon detection method. By adjusting the holding current, improved signal recordings have been achieved, with the coherence time rising from an initial 100 microseconds to 200 microseconds after Rb atom cooling.

Let the monoid of finite words, denoted as $\Sigma^*$, be defined over the alphabet $\Sigma$. It has been demonstrated that the MacNeille completion of this monoid, when viewed as a commutative semigroup with a defined order, can be represented by a specific type of closed set - those of regular expressions in positive letters from $\Sigma$. This is accomplished by developing a direct mapping from the original monoid into the monoid of set-regular expressions, for which a normal form is established. Subsequently, it is shown that the MacNeille completion is isomorphic to the closure of the regular expressions following a specific closure operation.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach is highly effective in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also demonstrating success in generating novel compounds that exhibit desired characteristics.

This paper explores the application of the Conditional Variational Approximation method in tackling complex continuous-time optimization problems. By leveraging a robust and simplified framework, the approach introduces a manageable number of parameters to approximate any problem. The parameters are adjusted to converge to the true solution of the problem. The paper also presents a new method for conditioning on trajectories and develops an approach to handle control variables, which is demonstrated with two case studies. These include a continuous-time Lasso problem and a control problem with unbounded actions, for which conditional approximations and algorithms are derived and experimentally evaluated.

A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. We identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, providing a comprehensive classification up to isomorphism.

In the context of high-dimensional linear regression, our analysis centers on the Bayesian approach using data-driven priors derived from [1]. Notably, these priors exhibit beneficial posterior contraction characteristics and efficient computational requirements. Building upon this foundation, our research expands on the existing theoretical frameworks by accommodating the scenario of unknown error variance under a sparsity assumption, ultimately demonstrating model selection consistency, optimal contraction rates, and satisfying the conditions of the Bernstein von Mises theorem via a multivariate t-distribution analysis.

To minimize energy consumption for machining, we examined the feed rate and cutting speed's influence, as governed by an empirical equation. An optimization framework, centered on minimizing energy consumption, was established with the cutting parameters and tool life as variables. These parameters were optimized under constraints including tool life and part dimensions. Various methods, such as RSM, a traditional quadratic approach, and a genetic algorithm, were applied to the problem. The results showed that energy consumption is most significantly affected by the feed rate, and we found a more energy-efficient machining strategy, with the genetic algorithm providing the best outcome.

The spectral dimension of a weighted graph is an exponent that describes the random walk's behavior on the graph, whereas the Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension of the graph's distance is an invariant characteristic. We present a counterexample disproving a previously held inequality concerning these dimensions, particularly for fractals lacking scale symmetry, as well as establish a condition under which the inequality holds in scale-symmetric graphs.

Utilizing the principles of $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing, we introduce a model for $Y(4230)$ that incorporates this phenomenon. Our model is consistent with existing data, and we find that the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ poles within the $Y(4230)$ resonance yield distinct outcomes. Also presented is the possibility of $Y(4230)$ being composed of $\eta$ and $\eta'$ poles in an approximately 50:50 ratio.

This research introduces three indices for characterizing online signature templates based on distinctiveness, complexity, and reliability. 
Distinctiveness is evaluated through statistical analysis of signature features, 
while complexity is determined by examining the trace of the signature. 
Both measures have been validated using a dataset containing signatures from individuals who performed them multiple times. 
The reliability index quantifies the consistency with which individual signers execute their signatures and is assessed using the standard deviation of signature patterns. 
The study's results show a correlation between reliability index values and average intraclass correlation coefficients for signature patterns. 
In addition, the paper provides analysis of how these three indices vary across different signers and their signature templates.

We investigated four-point amplitude calculations in the most fundamental string theory examples featuring T-fold backgrounds with six supersymmetries, discovering that their perturbative spectra possess an enhanced level of symmetry. This level of symmetry level is governed by groups such as $D_4$, $E_6$ and $E_7$. We demonstrated that the amplitude's $s,t,u$ symmetry holds for this example and derived a key property relating the external states helicities to the amplitude's Hermitian properties. Furthermore, our considerations led us to speculate on the potential existence of non-perturbative T-orient orbifients exhibiting six supersymmetries in the four examples studied.

Theoretical investigations have been carried out to examine how a single mobile dopant behaves in a half-filled Hubbard model on the triangular lattice, particularly in areas where it experiences significant resistance. Findings suggest that when a dopant becomes part of the resonance valence bond state, it significantly alters the surrounding short-range magnetic properties, a phenomenon known as magnetic dressing that weakens as the dopant's mobility increases. This is supported by various many-body methods, including variational wave functions and numerical results from path integral methods, which also demonstrate that a mobile dopant prefers to be located at points of higher coordination. Notably, a mobile dopant can be associated with a specific type of magnetic order that emerges through the breaking of local resonance valence bonds. These outcomes are comparable to those seen in cuprate materials in their hole-doped and held at a specific doping level.

We developed a comprehensive nucleosynthetic yield table for elements up to nickel, covering massive stars and asymptotic giant branch stars. This novel table accounts for various stellar evolution models, including the effects of rotation, convective processes, and core mass. For a thorough understanding, we compared our computed nucleosynthetic yields to prior studies and analyzed the influence of rotation and convective mechanisms on elemental yields. Our analysis shows that rotational effects are particularly significant in producing nitrogen within a specific mass range of stars. Additionally, we evaluated and compared our computed nucleosynthetic yields to prior studies of cosmic nucleosynthesis and the interstellar medium. Our computed nitrogen yields reveal that primary yields from AGB stars may be comparable to those produced by massive stars, which has significant implications for interpreting observations and simulations of galaxy formation and the nitrogen cycle within the universe.

Multilingual individuals often seamlessly switch between languages while communicating, a phenomenon known as code-switching, which has been extensively studied in linguistics but remains under-researched in NLP. This research aims to enhance our comprehension of code-switching through a new, data-driven framework. Our approach involves creating a comprehensive English-Hindi and code-switching corpus of nearly 200K sentences. Employing a BERT-based model, we achieve state-of-the-art results on existing English-Hindi and code-switching datasets, as well as on our newly established English-Hindi and code-switching corpus. Ultimately, our findings underscore the significance of incorporating code-switching into NLP datasets and models to better serve multilingual communities.

Biomedical datasets are often presented in the form of intricate graphs. The success of representation learning on graphs has propelled a surge of breakthroughs in biomedical machine learning, yet a clear understanding of its applications in this field is lacking. This review delves into the fundamental concepts of graph representation learning and highlights its notable achievements across the biomedical and life sciences sectors, showcasing a range of innovative methods that leverage graph representation learning effectively. Furthermore, it identifies promising prospects for further research and development within the sector, highlighting potential avenues for enhancing existing methods and discovering new opportunities for application.

Weakly Interacting Massive Particles may be captured within compact stars like white dwarfs, causing an increase in star luminosity through an annihilation reaction. This phenomenon could lead to a modification in the properties of the white dwarf cooling curve, which is usually used to determine star age and evolution. Although the concept of WIMP-induced modification to the white dwarf cooling curve was initially proposed, it wasn't a major focus in previous studies. This research further investigates the impact of WIMP capture and capture rate uncertainties on a white dwarf's cooling curve using a one-M$_\odot$ white dwarf as an example. The findings suggest that WIMP-induced modification to the white dwarf cooling curve could potentially be observed with current technology, leading to an incorrect interpretation of the white dwarf's age and evolution.

This study reveals that sharing images online can compromise one's privacy, prompting the development of an innovative tool - the Graph Privacy Advisor - to measure image privacy by analyzing an individual's online presence. The model leverages structured online data and interprets it using NLP, answering a user's query about the presence of a given individual in their own online network. The proposed system is tested on a dataset of graphs representing user profiles and demonstrates that an increasing amount of online data is privacy-sensitive. In contrast to conventional privacy-sensitivity assessments, the GPA evaluates images within their contextual framework. Moreover, the system is applicable beyond the initial testing scope, proving effective on data collected through web crawling, private datasets, and Facebook profiles.

We analyze the interaction between a quantum radiator and its own past, confined within a limited time frame, represented by a region of spacetime, called a "box." When the radiator's field and trajectory are treated classically, our study reveals that for large distances, the radiation action function linearly depends on a specific time delay between the radiator and its past, similar to a quantum delay operator we previously created. However, unlike the quantum version, our delay concept is entirely based on classical principles, yet leads to the same mathematically equivalent equations for probability amplitudes of interference. These findings allow us to better understand the nature of delay in radiation processes and provide new insights for improving approximate calculation methods. We also examine two types of radiator trajectories - one that is determined by delay and the other that is independent of it - and compare them by calculating the interference patterns of a neutron or photon neutron interferometer, as an example. When the delays of the two arms of the interferometer are similar, we find that both types of trajectories provide the same results, with differences of less than the ethereal energy. Nevertheless, when there is only delay in one arm, we find that differences between these two models can be as significant as the difference in delays, indicating distinct physical meaning and a need for solving the equations of delay exactly.

Measurements of charged-particle fragmentation in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions at the LHC are carried out with data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. Fragmentation functions, which relate jet energy to the sum of the fragments, are determined using both proton-proton and photon-tagged events. Additionally, fragmentation functions in inclusive jet events and lead-lead events are also measured. A higher average x_j value is observed in photon-tagged events than in proton-proton events with the same kinematic conditions. Within experimental uncertainties, no discrepancies are found between proton-proton, photon-tagged, and inclusive jet fragmentation functions. However, a noticeably harder pattern is observed in lead-lead collisions when adjusted for scale. These collisions exhibit a 10-20% increase in low-x_j fragmentation, and a 10-20% decrease in high-x_j fragmentation.

The CP2K program package, often seen as an extension of the Car-Parrinello method, has been developed over recent years with significant advancements in molecular dynamics simulations. Our recent updates have opened a highly-efficient and scalable multi-zonal native quantum/force-field molecular dynamics simulation pathway. This carries over from an earlier version, now enhanced to perform large-scale native simulations at unprecedented speeds. In this work, different native zone distributions and methods for calculating plane-wave kinetic energy and electrostatic potentials are examined. Our results show that a native zone positioned in the middle of a double-grid arrangement yields better outcomes than placement at the boundary for double-grid setups, especially with respect to minimizing electrostatic artifacts. The examination of various electrostatic potential smoothing techniques plane-wise, in addition to the conventional CW4 style, has led to the discovery that separating electrostatic and kinetic propagation and employing the simpler constant weights (CW0) scheme can be sufficient. This opens the door for the development of new, faster and more accurate methods for determining electrostatic potentials.

Small solar eruptions known as nanoflares may hold the key to explaining the solar corona's high temperatures due to the potential release of vast magnetic energy, potentially leading to the powerful solar flare explosions that scientists study today.  Research into the solar corona often involves the use of data collected by the extreme ultraviolet imaging spectrograph on the Solar Orbiter, which provides valuable insights into the dynamics of solar eruptions.  A study utilized such data to observe a nanoflare occurring in a solar feature called a pseudo-hole, which involved analyzing a flare's expansion and cooling behavior captured in extreme ultraviolet images.  The results revealed that the nanoflare erupted at high speeds, exceeding 100 km per second, suggesting that such eruptions could significantly influence the solar corona's structure and behavior.

In machine learning, particularly in natural language processing and computer vision, data augmentation has been effectively utilized to enhance model performance and resist overfitting. Nevertheless, no similar method has been developed for graph neural networks until now. Given the immense growth in applications involving complex graph structures, such as bioinformatics and social network analysis, there is a pressing need for graph data augmentation techniques. In this research, we introduce a novel method that increases the density of existing dense regions in a social network, and apply it to two social influence prediction contests. Our experiments demonstrate that our technique consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly when combined with other methods and data.

In 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories, complexity research has been conducted within multiple frameworks.  We discover that a universal pattern emerges when evaluating state complexity using the numerical path following approach for specific families of states consisting of local operator insertions within the light cone. We establish this pattern through two independent methods. Furthermore, we examine how this state complexity relates to the underlying CFT parameters. Our findings also shed light on the complexity of certain CFT states via the Konishi mode and contribute to understanding complexity within minimal models.

This research addresses the development of an efficient method for tracking the position and orientation of moving objects in various types of data, such as images and radar readings. A novel mathematical framework is presented that allows us to determine the minimum possible error in estimating the position of these objects over time. This position includes not only their location but also their orientation in space. To illustrate the method, we examine a specific problem involving the tracking of objects in two-dimensional images with a constant movement pattern. Based on our analysis, we designed a new estimator capable of accurately predicting the position of the object in subsequent frames. Notably, in ideal circumstances, the accuracy of this estimator reaches the lowest possible error rate allowed by the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound. To handle situations where the assumption of constant movement doesn't hold, we created a solution that tracks the position of the object frame by frame using a lower bound on error rates. This research provides a general approach applicable to a wide range of problems in posé estimation used in object tracking, recognition, and navigation techniques.

This report is a summary of a workshop of the same name held in Cambridge in 2018. The events outlined in this document are a continuation of a 2012 scout report under the sponsorship of the Dark Sector Science Program of the US Department of Energy. A full copy of the report can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.06127.

Researchers have discovered an instance of same-sign W boson pair production in proton-proton collisions. By analyzing data collected by the ATLAS experiment at a high-energy proton-proton collision level of 13 TeV, they found evidence supporting theoretical predictions, particularly for beyond-the-Standard-Model interactions. The study focused on events featuring specific characteristics, including identical lepton charges, high transverse momentum, and low missing momentum. Notably, the findings exhibited a notable discrepancy with the predictions made by the standard model, with events exhibiting greater frequencies than anticipated. Furthermore, this result align with the predictions made for beyond-the-Standard-Model interactions, with the probability of such outcomes occurring due to statistical fluctuations being extremely low, at a 2.8 standard deviation level.

This paper investigates the potential of color-plus-mono dual-camera systems to enhance low-light image quality, where each camera captures a distinct image. A previously published method by the authors leverages information from the mono camera to de-noise the color image across separate spatial and chromatic dimensions. In a new approach, color consistency between the two cameras is exploited to connect a low-res color image from the color channel with a high-res image from the color channel through a series of transformations. Specifically, a series of convolutions upsample a low-res color image to a high-res one while enforcing color consistency with a color component from the color image and a series of convolutions downsample a high-res one from the color channel to a low-res one. A previously published method by the authors previously leveraged information from a mono camera to de-noise a color image across separate spatial and chromatic dimensions. In a color-plus-mono system, the potential to improve color quality is maximized by utilizing a color consistency constraint between color images from the color and mono cameras to link a low-res image from the color channel to a high-res one through a series of transformations. Specifically, a previously published method by the authors previously leveraged information from a color component from the color image and a series of transformations. Specifically, a previously published method by the authors previously leveraged information from a color component from the color image and a series of transformations.

We examined the performance of three distinct dark energy (DE) parametrizations in light of various recent observational datasets. By utilizing CosmoMC for a Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis, we evaluated these models against a combination of datasets including Planck 2018, lensing, supernovae, and non-lensing CMB data, which led to an estimate of the clustering of matter. Interestingly, lensing plays a crucial role in narrowing down the uncertainty in our findings and our results indicate a potential inconsistency in lensing at approximately two-sigma level.

The advent of automated software tools has significantly influenced traditional maintenance processes, which has led to the emergence of a new idea known as meta-maintenance, which encompasses reflecting upon and adjusting the use of automation tools themselves to ensure effective maintenance outcomes. To establish a foundation for the meta-maintenance research area, this paper provides a comprehensive framework that enables maintenance tools creators to conduct an initial evaluation of their instruments through a detailed meta-maintenance analysis. By employing our analysis, it's possible to identify both the positive contributions and areas for improvement of a specific tool, ultimately allowing for optimized versions that better serve the overall maintenance process. Our case study evaluates the BLM-Beta meta-maintenance analysis of a specific automated bug-fixing tool designed for C# applications, which revealed that the BLM-Beta tool's performance fell short of initial expectations in terms of success rate and solution relevance. However, BLM-Beta also offered a substantial list of suggestions for potential enhancements to the bug-fixing tool, which has already led to the release of an updated version called BLM-Omega that integrates some of the recommended improvements.

The 2008 and 2009 observations of the eclipsing binary BD And, using the Las Cumbres Observatory network, enabled analysis of the system through light curves obtained in optical bands.  This study analyzed the light curves using the PHASE code, and found that the orbital inclination is 89.645$^\circ$, with eclipse depths of 0.026 in B and 0.019 in V.  Light curve analysis also revealed that the primary star may be a subgiant with a radius of 2.5 R$_{\odot}$, while the secondary star has a radius of 1.3 R$_{\odot}$.  Spectroscopic data from the LBO 6-m telescope in 2017 showed a radial velocity semi-amplitude of 14.7 km s$^{-1}$ for the system, which is consistent with earlier measurements.  Further analysis of the spectrum found that the spectral type of the primary star is K0-1, while the secondary star has a spectral type of G8.  Based on these findings, the mass and radius of the secondary star were calculated to be 1.03 M$_{\odot}$, 1.09 R$_{\odot}$, and 1.02 M$_{\odot}$, 1.30 R$_{\odot}$ for the primary star, respectively.

This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved introducing a Yamabe flow based on fractional curvature and demonstrating the existence of mild solutions. The current research expands on that study by establishing the convergence of the flow under certain data conditions within a broader framework. The new results are derived from an approach simplified by Struwe in his book.

Cross-domain recommendation has garnered significant interest due to its capability to leverage shared information across multiple domains to enhance recommendation effectiveness. Existing approaches primarily rely on a single shared space for multiple domains. Nevertheless, this strategy fails to take advantage of the unique characteristics of each domain that arise from their disparate user preferences and ratings. To rectify this limitation, we introduce a novel sparsity-based Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model. The model encompasses a shared multi-task learning framework along with a novel framework that enables collaboration among multiple domains for sparsity reduction and enhanced learning. The model's innovation lies in its adoption of a novel framework that allows for enhanced collaboration among multiple domains. The model's performance has been rigorously evaluated through comprehensive experiments on four real-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art baseline methods.

We establish that the deformation space of a sheaf over a smooth projective variety is defined by the first hypercohomology of a constructed complex for orthogonal and symplectic cases. Additionally, our study introduces an obstruction theory, which targets the second hypercohomology space.

Andrews and Merca's findings on even partitions with distinct parts, represented by a(n), have been expanded upon, and new research results are presented regarding partitions with distinct parts, but also limiting the multiplicity of each part. A proof using a modified version of Glaisher's concept is offered. The underlying generating functions for these new sequence families are derived and then utilized to validate previously stated formulas.

Given a set of samples with noise, we develop theoretical frameworks to construct the optimal finite-dimensional linear approximation space for an underlying target function under different performance metrics. The results show that in a noise-free environment, the optimal approximation space matches the target function, but with noisy data, a bias-variance trade-off arises, linking it to a specific range of the approximating space. We propose and mathematically validate two techniques to build this optimal space, and experimentally evaluate their efficacy on synthetic data using different noise levels and target functions, as well as on a diverse range of benchmark datasets, assessing their impact on various machine learning models and metrics.

To investigate the transportation and yield formation of the $J/\psi$, $\psi(2S)$, $B_c$ and bottomonium ions in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, a comprehensive evaluation is performed. This assessment incorporates two primary parameters, a time-dependent temperature function and the bottom quark interaction with the hot medium, which is modeled through the constituent quark interaction and the Debye-screening effect. A detailed comparison with experimental data from the RHIC and LHC is conducted in multiple scenarios to determine the transport parameters, including the bottom quark interaction cross-section, the heavy quark scattering off the Debye-screened gluons, and the temperature-dependent Debye-screening mass. A detailed analysis of time- and space-dependent temperature and bottom quark distribution is carried out in different scenarios to examine the transport of heavy mesons and compare their results with pre-measurement data in various scenarios.

The occurrence of local moments in systems with disorder and the resulting magnetic correlations in insulators can be studied through a theoretical framework. In one dimension, we have developed a new method to examine magnetic correlations in systems with strong disorder. Our method involves calculating the magnetic susceptibility from the energy levels of the system, which we obtain from one-dimensional Hubbard and Anderson models. Our results show that while spin correlations decay in insulators with disorder, they do so in a way that preserves local moments. We also find that this decay follows a power law for certain parts of the system. Moreover, we discovered that both the power and the coefficient of this power law vary depending on the strength of disorder. Our findings align with previous research on magnetic correlations in systems with disorder.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) was initially introduced for abelian groups and later extended to non-abelian groups with specific properties. A general application of OGS was limited to solvable groups of a particular depth. A generalization was sought for groups that share properties with non-abelian groups of prime square order. A new outcome reveals the constraints on such groups based on their commutator subgroups' order and provides examples that exemplify the discovered constraints. Furthermore, a code based on the ordered generating sequences was explored for potential use as a cryptosystem given the significant differences in the representation of group elements.

This study investigates kink soliton patterns within scalar field interactions, applying theory to introduce two new fields with breaking symmetry. These fields give rise to a model with two key parameters that can be adjusted to explore various soliton types. Through calculations, it's been found that specific parameter values lead to the emergence of new soliton patterns with distinct topological properties. These properties can be adjusted by fine-tuning the parameters, resulting in transitional periods that contain multiple kinks. Notably, this model also exhibits a tri-kink soliton, which was previously unobserved in similar tri-scalar field interactions.

Robots that learn from observations in real-world environments using inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) face a significant challenge when experts perform irrelevant actions. These irrelevancies can make it difficult for the algorithm to identify the true objectives. A new IRL approach called SPOT-IRL has been developed to overcome this limitation. By filtering out unwanted data and focusing on observations relevant to the task at hand, SPOT-IRL is able to robustly identify expert goals even in the presence of significant noise. By combining a sparsity-promoting objective with the maximum margin inverse reinforcement learning (MMIRL) algorithm, SPOT-IRL can effectively separate valuable from unvaluable data and provide a robust solution to IRL problems. Experimental results demonstrate that SPOT-IRL outperforms existing methods by a substantial margin.

Given a subgroup $H$ of the fundamental group of a space $X$, we develop the concept of a strong $H$-SLT space by adapting the definition by Zhang and Wu. Our main results demonstrate that any strong $H$-SLT space with a connected cover corresponding to $H$ satisfies the condition for the corresponding map to be a covering projection. In addition, we establish new criteria to identify strong $H$-SLT spaces by examining local properties. Furthermore, our study provides examples of strong $H$-SLT spaces that do not satisfy the weaker $H$-SLT property defined by Cao and Wu.
