This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, focusing on flat general rotation surfaces characterized by a 1-type Gauss map. Additionally, it's established that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with this distinct Gauss map is a Lie group if and only if it's a Clifford torus.

A vast amount of unannotated videos are readily available, and integrating these resources can significantly enhance the performance of deep neural networks on semantic segmentation tasks. We propose a novel self-supervised learning approach that utilizes depth estimation from unlabelled videos for pre-training. By incorporating this unsupervised depth estimation for metric learning, we can obtain a more universally applicable model. Experiments conducted on various datasets reveal that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in a multitude of scenarios, in terms of both unanchored and anchored training methodologies. Specifically, our model demonstrates superior performance on ImageNet with unsupervised depth estimation, outperforming existing unanchored approaches by 3.6% and surpassing anchored methods with 0.6% improvement. Furthermore, our model exhibits a notable enhancement in performance on ADE20K and CityScapes, with improvements of 1.0% and 1.7%, respectively.

The emergence of data-driven storytelling has led to a heightened interest in generating compelling narratives from large datasets. Inference-driven time-series visualization, or time-telling, is a relatively unexplored area that aims to automatically create insightful stories from time-series data. To address the need for more robust and data-driven visualization tools, we introduce TCube, a comprehensive framework for the visual analysis of time-series timeframes. TCube's multivariate analysis enables users to discover and visualize interconnected subsets of time-series variables, referred to as timeframes. TCube's innovative features include a three-dimensional visual representation called the Timeframe Cube, dynamic heatmaps, and synchronized playback capabilities. TCube empowers users to manually explore and manually select important variables within time-series data, as well as manually manipulate Timeframe Cube visualizations to gain deeper insights. Through real-world case studies, we demonstrate TCube's capability to transform complex time-series data into actionable stories and insights.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved a 
two-standard deviation measurement for CP violation in neutral B mesons 
($B^0$ and $B^{0}_{s}$) and also documented two-significant deviation 
measurements of CP violation in bottom b-hadrons. These measurements 
relate to the matter-antimatter asymmetry within the universe and are 
connected to the effectiveness of the Standard Model. The experiment's 
results also provide information about rare decays and sparsely occurring 
processes, offering potential insights into new particles beyond the Standard 
Model. This article presents two-significant deviation measurements of CP 
violation in several $B$-meson systems and evaluates the most recent results 
of rare decays involving bottom-b-hadrons.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

This study provides a global well-posedness proof in the $H^1$ space for strictly hyperbolic equations with mildly blowing up coefficients. The resulting estimates show that the solution's solution in $H^1$ norm is bounded by $C(T)\cdot\|u_0\|_{H^1}$ to fourth power of $|\log T|$. The method involves exploiting the equation's hyperbolic structure through a combination of high-low high frequency decomposition, and making use of high frequency solutions' high time regularity.

This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These character combinations result in significant morphological differences, leading to a high degree of ambiguity in Japanese word segmentation. To address this challenge, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into account the unique requirements of this language. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, a dataset of Japanese word segmentation was assembled and used to compare the performance of different neural network models. The experimental results indicate that the proposed model is a viable solution for Japanese word segmentation.

On Stack Overflow, external knowledge is an integral part of link sharing activities. A substantial portion of contributions involve annotated external references. This paper explores a novel approach to automatically extracting and managing links along with their accompanying comments. Our method achieves a 57% F1 score in correctly identifying resources, and an impressive 87% F1 score in accurately assigning comments to those resources. A resulting database of annotated links has been created, encompassing a diverse range of topics, to facilitate further research into link management. Evaluations demonstrate the capability of our proposed strategy to enhance link management quality on Stack Overflow by reducing redundancy and boosting clarity.

Galactic rotation curves are analyzed to determine the influence of Self-Interacting Dark Matter (SIDM) on observed structures, particularly from the inner to outer galactic regions. This study focuses on SIDM models with varying cross-sections to understand their effect on observed galactic features. By comparing these models to Cold Dark Matter (CDM) simulations, it's evident that SIDM with a cross-section of up to 0.5 sq. cm does not significantly impact the rotation curve's profile. However, SIDM models may leave noticeable imprints beyond a radius of 10 kiloparsecs, with a cross-section of 2 sq. cm or more. It is essential to consider that SIDM interactions do not respond to Baryonic Feedback Processes (BFP), and their effects are primarily observed in the galactic's outer regions.

Although climate change is widely acknowledged by scientists, common language remains
ineffective at prompting individuals to reduce their carbon footprints. Our study
leverages concepts from network theory and information theory to devise a framework
for describing and disseminating climate change. We utilize this framework to develop
an optimized strategy for climate change communication, one that maximizes the
number of receptive individuals by tailoring messages to specific communities and
distributing them optimally across various channels of influence in a society's
network. The model is applied to a U.S. community with two target groups - those
open to environmental actions and those who are not - and is further applied to
optimize the overall understanding of the climate change within that society.

A technique to extract symptoms from handwritten clinical notes, even across different healthcare facilities, involves utilizing transfer learning with diverse network models and a diverse sample of individual physician-patient interactions as new training data. By fine-tuning these models on new datasets, our approach achieves comparable accuracy in extracting symptoms, allowing for seamless deployment in a wide range of healthcare institutions without extensive retraining. Furthermore, our method surpasses the accuracy of human annotators in evaluating handwritten notes, demonstrating significant potential for improving patient care and reducing errors in assessments.

Deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising technique for developing end-to-end autonomous driving systems. However, its practical application is hampered by the high cost of collecting driving datasets for supervised pre-training. We propose a novel, novel approach to addressing this issue by incorporating deep reinforcement learning into the driving process. Our model-driven predictive following module is designed to learn the dynamics of vehicles in an unsupervised manner. We evaluate the following performance of this module under two distinct driving scenarios: a random following scenario and a following of a lead vehicle scenario. Our results indicate that this module is capable of adapting to various vehicles under the random following scenario and successfully models the lead vehicle under the following of a lead vehicle scenario.

In recent years, AI-driven solutions have demonstrated exceptional performance across various domains, largely thanks to advancements in hardware and computational power. Initially fueled by Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), researchers recently revived interest in Neuromorphic Computing, which drew inspiration from biological neurons to create energy-efficient systems. By utilizing Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), these systems offer faster computational capabilities with reduced computational demands. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of SPINNAKER, a rigorous simulator for SNNs that incorporates learning algorithms and diverse hardware configurations. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SNNs trained with backpropagation across multiple datasets, utilizing different neuron models and synaptic models within the SPINNAKER environment to simulate ANNs and compare their equivalence.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a finite temperature condition, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we determined the equation of state for the thermodynamic variables of spin-polarized strange quark matter and then utilized these outcomes to construct a phase diagram in the $TR$ vs $B^{1/2}$ plane, which is specific to spin-polarized strange quark matter. Lastly, a comparative analysis was performed between the phase diagrams of spin-polarized and unpolarized strange quark matter to understand the influence of spin-polarization and ferromagnetic properties on their phases.

A growing number of programs and services now utilize unmonitored personal devices, such as smartphones and laptops, to execute tasks in parallel. This concept, known as volunteer computing, has demonstrated value in scientific research, data analysis, and film rendering. To expand its influence, we developed Pando, a user-friendly and protocol-agnostic volunteer computing tool analogous to Hadoop. Pando's simplicity lies in its ability to run on unaltered Python code, and its scalability is limited only by the availability of devices. We have integrated Pando with multiple services, including Aperture 3 for image editing and SETI@home for data analysis. This paper outlines Pando's features and illustrates its efficacy through case studies showcasing its potential in various fields.

A computational method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, using an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified eigenproblem equation.  By utilizing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then employs the collected information to produce approximations for the desired eigenvalues through interpolation techniques. Both real and complex eigenvalues are addressed with specific sampling and interpolation methods tailored to each case. Relevant theories and processes from approximation theory underpin this solution strategy. Relevant numerical tests demonstrate the solution's performance.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence between a broad class of intermediate $\beta$-transformations and modified greedy $\beta$-transformations with a gap at zero, for certain values of $\beta$. These transformations are represented as graph-mappings, and we obtain a characterization of their periodic behavior, leading to a description of the set of points with a given gap under the inverse image. We also define the concept of completely uniform distribution with respect to a gap and prove a distribution theorem for image points of such sets. Furthermore, under specific conditions, we show that the measure of this set remains unchanged along a sequence of nested gaps at zero, and investigate its limiting behavior.

We've found that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and matter fields represented as vectors confine, resulting from monopole condensation and the quark bilinear breaking $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry down to $SO(N_{F})$. Our findings derive from an ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric theory, specifically with anomaly-mediated supersymmetry breaking.

Tree ensemble models are widely regarded as inherently interpretable due to their visualizable decision rules, yet this interpretability loses relevance when an explanation is tied to specific model instances rather than generalizing across them. This study addresses this issue by developing a new explanation framework, namely Disentangled Attribution Curves, that can uncover clear and consistent explanations for tree-based methods' predictions by using disentangled representations. These representations, obtained through an unsupervised learning approach called Disentangled Flow Matching, isolate specific patient characteristics to explain a model's decision. Based on these representations, our Disentangled Attribution Curves method determines how the model leverages each patient characteristic to make a decision. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by comparing it to established attribution methods and showing that Disentangled Attribution Curves can reveal more consistent and reliable explanations for their predictions on both synthetic and real-world data, such as in predicting heart failure from electronic health records.

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially reveal confidential information. Recent advancements in execution environments like Intel's Software Guard Extensions and Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) offer an alternative, with memory encryption providing some degree of privacy. However, this approach has a significant flaw - models transmitted by participants can intentionally or inadvertently cause models within the TEE to leak information. To rectify this issue, we've developed a framework called Privately Executed Federated Learning (PEFL) that combines TEE capabilities with theoretically-proven privacy measures. This framework ensures model parameters are kept within the TEE, where they're processed using secure methods, thus preventing any leaks. To address performance bottlenecks, we've incorporated compression techniques and theoretical analyses, showing our framework results in smaller models and faster training. Experimental results show that the privacy-compliant models trained using PEFL achieve comparable accuracy to non-private models, and outperform previous attempts at achieving private federated learning with TEE.

The embedded systems industry is massive and encompasses a diverse range of applications that require external peripheral interaction, leading to complex systems with external dependencies. This interaction contributes to numerous interaction faults that complicate embedded software development and testing, particularly when simulating and co-simulating with physical hardware. This research aims to tackle this challenge by creating a fault injection technique that utilizes a next-generation Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) emulator to artificially introduce and simulate system failures at the hardware level, thereby enhancing embedded software testing and improving its reliability. By developing a novel hardware-based approach to mimic physical failure injections, we can more accurately replicate physical failure behaviors and increase the reliability of embedded software in various industries. This paper outlines a method for co-simulating and inverting control signals on an FPGA-based industry emulator to replicate external peripheral interaction failure injections, followed by a case study utilizing a Xilinx ZCU102 industry board to validate the proposed technique.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops, which utilizes control flow graphs to automatically determine optimal system call filters for containerized applications. These system call filters are used to flag anomalous behavior in real-time without the need for extensive configuration by operations engineers. Unlike previous static analysis methods, Timeloops employs dynamic tracing during a safe test run of the application in a sandboxed container to accurately identify essential system calls and accurately detect anomalies in real-world scenarios. By using machine learning, Timeloips can handle a wide range of applications and correctly capture the impact of complex system call interactions. The approach is specifically adapted for microservices applications that run on popular orchestration platforms like Kubernetes. The effectiveness of Timeloops is demonstrated through a case study of an image processing application with multiple services and an attack simulation on the application.

Advanced neural network architectures, such as convolutional and transposed convolutional layers, can be understood and analyzed through a generalized approach to tilt operators. Researchers have established a framework for universal approximation using linear classifiers in complex product spaces, regardless of the underlying manifold's properties. Furthermore, it has been proven that these linear classifiers have a robust ability to represent functions across diverse geometric environments, regardless of the specific type of manifold involved. The findings also hold true for specific applications, such as classifying images of handwritten digits, but this code is not yet available for public use.

This introduction focuses on stochastic Model Predictive Control methods that account for uncertainty in constraints, illustrated through a linear system under unpredictable conditions. The corresponding Matlab code is also accessible online for reference purposes.

This paper introduces a novel concept of compressive learning, where measurements are taken in a compressive manner to significantly reduce computational complexity in learning tasks. By leveraging the property of sparsity and structure in data, our proposed approach enables efficient learning processes. This is achieved by utilizing a sparsity-promoting regularized least square problem as a base model and integrating it into our compressive learning process. This reformulation leads to a novel transform-domain compressive learning method. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through experiments on speech recognition, linear regression, and binary classification problems, where it exhibits superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and immigration, we examine a modified Lotka-Volterra model with multiple competing species on a finite domain of size $L$, where species can enter through the boundaries. An average of $I$ species immigrate per unit time, bringing new competitors to the system. Over the long term, the model reveals a novel phase transition driven by immigration, where a continuous phase of species coexistence gives way to a discontinuous phase in which a single species dominates. Using both mean-field theory and numerical simulations, we find that critical immigration levels depend on system size in all directions. As immigration increases, there's a significant shift in the winning species due to this phase transition. Curiously, our model exhibits another transition when immigrating species have lower growth rates than incumbent ones, with the system now selecting between a cluster of CO2-emitting species and a suite of species that absorb CO2, with the point of transition separating these two groups of species.
We prove that von Neumann algebras associated with compact regions within abelian quantum double models have infinite type $II$.

To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we suggest applying a time-modulated auxiliary magnetic field, controlled by a feedback loop, which compensates for the system's dissipation and improves entanglement. Our analysis reveals that this proposed approach accounts for the loss mechanisms within the system, leading to a higher level of entanglement. Additionally, by adjusting the strength of the time-modulated field through a feedback loop, we can extend the range of parameters that produce entanglement. The degree of entanglement achieved can be quantified using the logarithmic negativity, which we demonstrate experimentally in a range of time-modulated field amplitudes that exhibit a macroscopic level of entanglement. Our findings offer a means to fine-tune and optimize entanglement in future experiments featuring time-modulated auxiliary magnetic fields.

We've obtained one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color and spin spaces, applicable to all five scenarios: $q \to qq'\bar{q}'$, $q \to qq̄'\bar{q}$, $q \to q'\bar{q}\bar{q}'$, $q \to \bar{q}q\bar{q}'$, and $q \to \bar{q}\bar{q}q\bar{q}'$. We've also derived a general formula for $n$-flavor $q \to qq'\bar{q}'$ splittings. These results are useful in developing efficient subtraction methods and matched computations that involve subtractions and power corrections beyond fixed-order perturbation theory.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local rings, and this concept is currently being used within Singular software implementation. Furthermore, a relevant theorem based on Greenberg's Strong Approximation theorem has also been introduced and applied to the realm of one-dimensional local rings.

The positions of celestial bodies in the sky have long been essential to human life, guiding our understanding of seasons, navigation, and timekeeping. The dynamics of the Sun and Moon have historically been of significant interest, with their daily and monthly movements offering profound insights. The rich Islamic civilization made notable contributions to astronomy, with their observatories making precise astronomical measurements. The seminal 10th-century Zij al-Sindhijri astronomical treatise contained a innovative graph known as the Dishah, or hourly movement of the Sun, depicting the Moon's hourly movement as well. The original Dishah has been the subject of restoration and recreation efforts for over a century. The Tiling Journal journal article presents a novel approach to recreating the Dishah using parameterized parabolic and elliptical arcs, ensuring mathematical continuity and preserving the original's aesthetic and functional aspects.

This paper addresses an issue in near-field wireless communication by introducing an innovative near-field wireless communication technique. It optimizes a decentralized D2D communication system enhanced by an intelligent reflecting surface, where a cooperative relay helps underutilized D2D links increase their throughputs in a competitive environment with a backhaul connection. We develop a innovative, self-learning strategy using Q-learning to simultaneously determine the D2D throughputs and relay assistance, focusing on a achievable rate measure. This innovative strategy allows the D2D links to learn and optimize their throughputs and the relay's beamforming without interacting with each other or the base station. The proposed strategy allows the system to achieve near-optimal D2D throughputs and sum-throughputs, verified by a simulation study.

The surge in telework due to confinement measures is creating a need for a videoconferencing tool that can introduce new features, such as the capability to observe a sample's response in two dimensions using Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) data. 
An attempt has been made to develop a simple 3D representation method based on a spatial analysis of the LDV measurement coordinates to visualize two-dimensional (2D) laser Doppler vibrometer responses. 
The underlying principle relies on the assumption that a test object's movement is confined within two dimensions. 
By calculating the angle between the varying measurement coordinates, it's possible to generate an 'heat map' and present these results in an animated format. 
Although not as precise as traditional methods, this approach provides a quick overview of activity on a 2D sample and could be useful in identifying fault lines or patterns. 
A video demonstration of an implementation of this technique is available on YouTube at the following link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4d9111111111.

The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities.  Notably, $\Phi'$ can be constructed from $\Phi$ using a general method, although in some instances it involves increasing the number of variables significantly.  The resulting models of $\Phi'$ from these constructions are specified, and we suggest that similar results might be achievable with a more minimal increase in the number of variables.  The proof involves introducing a general method to transform a binary relation into two symmetric binary relations.

We've proposed a novel electrostatic phase plate design for Transmission Electron Microscopes that can mitigate the negative impact of spherical aberration, by programmably correcting for it. Our simulations suggest that with this approach, a significant improvement in electron electron microscopy resolution can be achieved, surpassing the limitations imposed by the electron microscope's intrinsic aberration.

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified by tunneling dynamics, optical resonators, and atom-laser interactions.

This study employs the power of geometric formulas to develop a method for calculating the probabilities of n-step random walks in d-dimensional space. Our approach will be demonstrated for the case of a straight-line return to the starting point, and a new, generic formula will be proposed to determine the possible positions of the walk's endpoint after n steps in d-dimensional space.

In this research, we investigate the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes and their GCRs with quantum corrections. We utilize the GW and GM equations to derive the WDM black hole structure equation. Then, considering scalar field disturbances, we obtain WDM black hole quasinormal frequencies via the pseudospacetime metric approach. WDM black hole quasinormal frequencies exhibit dependence on fields $ \theta $ and $ \lambda $. WDM black hole quasinormal frequencies exhibit an increase in an absolute value as fields' quantum effects weaken.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context from written form. These systems can produce syntheses with repetitive prosody, which we aim to improve. Our solution involves incorporating written context into speech synthesis at the paragraph level. We focus on modeling paragraph-specific features that impact speech quality, such as the frequency of function words, and use this information to modulate prosody in speech. This research is part of a larger goal of speech synthesis that mirrors human-like expression.

We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models within the exponential family. We've rigorously evaluated our approach by comparing it with established methods on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in accurately selecting variables and recovering relevant structures.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to manipulation through adversarial examples. While vulnerabilities such as handling novel classes and configurations have been studied, less is known about their resilience to unexpected object orientations. This study investigates how to protect object classifiers from unforeseen rotations. We utilize the principle of data augmentation to create robust models by incorporating object rotation into the training process. Furthermore, we utilize the Graph Neural Network to develop a cross-domain object recognizer that can accurately identify objects across different datasets without requiring object segmentation. This method yields a notable improvement in performance for both novel rotations and cross-domain scenarios, outperforming comparable methods.

Climate change communication through social media is hindered by climate skeptics who utilize various tactics to block, divert, and overtake pro-climate messaging. One such tactic involves the dissemination of conspiracy theory information online. In this research, existing research on climate change and conspiracy theory dissemination online is synthesized. One crucial, yet underexplored area of this research concerns the social media behaviors of climate skeptics vs. believers. Our study utilized an online survey of diverse Facebook group members, revealing that climate change belief influences skepticism expression and sharing. Furthermore, those with a climate change skepticism tendency exhibit more climate-related conspiracy skepticism, are more inclined to engage with conspiracy-related content, and are more likely to share such information online, particularly among those who value freedom of speech. These findings provide insights into the digital strategies employed by climate skeptics to disseminate climate change denial and suggest avenues for further research into online climate change communication among diverse demographics.

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using data collected by the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This study involved searching for a specific two-jet and two-lepton signature accompanied by significant missing transverse momentum above 120 GeV within a specific time-frame following the collision. The investigation has yielded notable results, revealing new constraints on simplified models featuring dijet resonance and dark matter, as well as new limits on scalar and pseudoscalar mediators produced through dark current interactions. The observed data aligned with expected outcomes across a range of models, including dijet mediation models ranging from 0.15 to 1.0 PeV mass for scalar and pseudoscalar mediators, pseudoscalar dark matter with masses below 100 GeV, di-jet mediation models with specific mass and cross-section ranges, and scalar dark matter with masses below 100 GeV and a broad range of cross-sections.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work that demonstrates the feasibility of combining multiple treatment instruments with ranked preference data, we develop a new approach for the nonparametric estimation of treatment effects based on such instrument and preference information.  To identify treatment effects from this data, we utilize the characteristics of treatment-specific instrumental variables which influence a subset of treatment choices while leaving others unchanged.  These instruments enable us to express treatment-specific choice probabilities as functions of their impact on the treated.  We then establish a relationship between instrumental and treatment-specific information through an optimization condition that allows us to solve for treatment effects.  To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we develop an algorithm that alternately updates estimates of treatment effects and the underlying value function, enabling us to recover treatment specific effects from the estimated relationships.  To illustrate the utility of our approach, we reanalyze German university students' choice of educational institutions and fields of study, initially reported by Kirkeboen et al. (2016), and successfully estimate treatment effects for fields of study by incorporating data from two relevant instrumental variables.

To advance our understanding of matter's antiparticle states and prevent confusion with matter and holes, researchers need high-quality beams of slow-moving, relativistic antiparticles. Relativistic antiparticles are difficult to create due to annihilation with regular matter, limiting available beam types to those relativistic initially and inherently antinatural: antineutrons, positrons, and antiprotons. Our project involves developing a unique, relativistic electron-antiproton scattering experiment using a synchrotron radiation proton beam and a helicon plasma target to study fundamental properties of antiprotons. We will explore various beam-target interaction options to optimize outcomes and identify a viable beam-target combination and suitable scientific targets for future experiments.

Most of the known compact binary binaries (CBCs) discovered by LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA (VLK) operate within a larger triple system. We've developed a numerical model that investigates the behavior of such triples during a specific scenario where a third body acquires mass through accretion at a differential rate. This happens when a inner binary's components have an established mass ratio. We've found that in scenarios where a comparable mass is added to a small binary by a third body of similar mass, the accretion process doesn't have a substantial impact on the small binary. Conversely, when a significant mass is added to a small binary by a more massive third body, the accretion process can cause the small binary to gain mass. This leads to an increased merger time. Notably, in cases where a highly unequal mass ratio exists between the small binary and the third body, the accretion process can have a stabilizing effect. This leads to a decreased merger time. We've discovered that the rate at which mass is accreted has a more pronounced impact on the outcome when a unequal mass ratio exists. We've found that the accretion process can have either a positive or negative effect on the merger time of the small binary, with the magnitude of the change in the merger time for a given accretion rate being on the order of the same mass as the third body. We've concluded that to accurately assess the effect of mass growth on the merger

This paper examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, which can serve as foundational models for understanding cosmological and gravitational phenomena. We identify two intrinsic metrics that are intrinsically flat within a conformally flat spacetime structure. Additionally, we develop two novel coordinate systems to facilitate the visualization of these metric surfaces. We then explore a specific case where a spacetime is conformally flat but intrinsically flat from a non-conformal metric's perspective, revealing that such a spacetime must be a direct product of a 2D flat plane and a 2D curved spacetime, which itself must be either intrinsically flat or intrinsically curved.

This paper introduces a novel image segmentation task called Image Segmentation with Missing Labels, which focuses on classifying only a subset of pixels with missing labels. We propose a method that combines image segmentation and image restoration models to tackle this issue more efficiently. Our approach uses image segmentation to define a mask for the meaningful pixels and an image restoration model to reconstruct the background. By using our method, we can improve the performance of image segmentation and image restoration models on related tasks, such as image completion and image synthesis. Our experiment shows that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing methods on the CMU Multi-Person dataset.

Active Galactic Nuclei are expected to have a range of black hole masses and spins, which can be determined by analyzing their electromagnetic spectra. This research proposes using active X-ray and gamma-ray observations to create a database of black hole mass and spin. To do this, we developed a method for estimating the spin and mass of accretion black holes based on their hard X-ray and gamma-ray spectra, and applied it to a sample of Active Galactic Nuclei with known distances. The results show that our mathematical approach effectively predicts the spin and mass of black holes, but more observations are needed to refine our method. Ultimately, a large database of AGN parameters will be useful for studying the distribution of black hole masses and spins in the universe.

We introduce Fougere, a free and open-source Python tool capable of emulating different types of event-based neural systems on various platforms, including analog, digital, and computational neural networks. Fougere utilizes a range of existing emulators to offer a unified simple interface for defining and running these networks. Its key advantage is the ability to easily define and simulate different types of neural systems without having to write a lot of code. We highlight Fougere's features and how it surpasses other emulation frameworks in terms of flexibility and ease of use, with a focus on simulating continuous neural networks. Fougere's capabilities can be explored at: https://github.com/ibm-research/fougere.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated by stellar flares and observed through radio spectra that exhibit significant frequency modulation. We studied the evolution of a particular type-I noise storm associated with a small solar flare, using radio images at 149 MHz, and found two distinct evolution patterns. The first, commonly observed, features rapid increases and decreases in frequency, caused by changes in the particle beam's velocity or the stellar background fields. In contrast, the noise storm in question also showed a gradual increase in frequency, which was captured in images but not in existing solar type-I models. Our analysis suggests this slower evolution is a new finding and provides insights into the physical processes behind it through mathematical equations.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity.

The spherically symmetric merging of a cloud and a black hole is an ideal setting to study how high angular momentum affects mass accretion and black hole growth. A thorough examination is conducted using three distinct initial conditions for a rotating gas cloud and one evolving general relativistic black hole. As the merger occurs and respects angular momentum conservation, accretion ceases and a stable, disk-like structure forms around the black hole. Despite variations caused by numerical factors, a universal relationship emerges, describing how mass accretion rate depends on the initial specific angular momentum in these merging systems. Notably, in these merging scenarios, mass accretion can surpass limits set by standard thin disk models, even at substantial distances from the central object. This phenomenon holds practical implications for understanding black hole growth and galaxy evolution at large scales.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A long-term study of massive star hosts has been conducted to uncover potential patterns in their spatial distribution.  By analyzing 125 high-confidence massive star hosts from the literature, researchers found the majority reside within dense clusters.  However, 22 of these were discovered outside of any dense cluster environment, potentially indicating a new class of star formation.  Among these, 10 massive star hosts exhibited signs of being part of dense, obscured regions.  Furthermore, examination of their host galaxies revealed none belonged to extremely massive or star-forming categories, further supporting the idea that massive stars can form in various environments.  Detailed analysis of two host samples with numerous members found their mass distribution and initial mass function to be similar to other known massive star hosts.  Ultimately, further investigation of massive stars is needed to refine understanding of their spatial distribution and potential formation patterns.

This paper investigates the normalized ground state solution of the biharmonic Choquard type equation $\Delta^2 u-\lambda u=\kappa (I_\alpha*|u|^p)|u|^{p-2}u$ in $\mathbb{R}^4$. We demonstrate that for $\lambda\in(0,\infty)$ and $3\le p<5$, the normalized ground state solution $\mathcal{M}_\lambda c_\theta^{\lambda,p}\theta$ solution set in $H^2(\mathbb{R}^4)\cap H(\mathcal{M}_\lambda c_\theta^{\lambda,p}\theta)$. Here, $\kappa > 0$, $I_\alpha$ is the Riesz potential with $\alpha \in (0,4]$, and $H(\mathcal{M}_\lambda c_\theta^{\lambda,p}\theta)$ represents the $H^2(\mathbb{R}^4)$ Nehari manifold for this normalized ground state solution $\mathcal{M}_\lambda c_\theta^{\lambda,p}\theta$ in $H^2(\mathbb{R}^4)$. We also examine the stability of this normalized ground state solution $\mathcal{M}_\lambda c_\theta^{\lambda,p}\theta$ solution set in $H^2(\mathbb{R}^4)$.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are affected by factors such as age, water damage, and ink leakage, often become difficult to read. These documents may exhibit smudges that obscure legibility, making them unsuitable for automated restoration methods. A proposed mark detection algorithm uses the image gradient to identify large mark areas and leverage the binary mask for restore the PDF layer. However, to enhance the accuracy of the algorithm, a new approach is implemented to detect small mark areas via a binary mask and automatically adjust the JRecover parameters to optimize restoration results.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly transformed how Information is exchanged, making it crucial to convert machine-readable formats like the OCR technology can provide into a more accessible format for users. OCR technology has been successfully employed in extracting text from ID card images, allowing this information to be further analyzed. OCR technology's capabilities have also expanded to extracting key information from ID card images, which can then be utilized for authentication and data processing. This research explores the potential of using OCR technology to not only convert ID card images into text but also to extract essential personal information for authentication and analysis purposes.

In vehicular communications, accurate channel estimation is a critical factor for reliable data transmission. Due to the dynamic nature of channel conditions, frequent and precise channel tracking is required, which is contingent upon the optimal design of pilot allocations. While pilots are essential for channel estimation, they also consume limited system resources. Consequently, devising an efficient pilot allocation strategy is a crucial objective. A novel resource-constrained pilot allocation scheme for OFDM systems is proposed, which incorporates a flexible design of orthogonal cover sequences (OCS) pilots to enhance estimation accuracy while minimizing resource consumption. By optimizing the OCS pilot allocation, the scheme achieves a balance between performance and resource efficiency in frequency-selective channels. The effectiveness of the scheme is demonstrated through simulations, which show its ability to reduce the total number of pilots while maintaining or improving estimation accuracy. Furthermore, it exhibits a significant improvement in estimation performance compared to traditionally allocated pilots under the same resource constraints.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered significant interest within the machine learning community due to its numerous practical applications in computer vision and computer graphics. Despite this focus on method development, colorization models developed to date, while available, have not been consistently evaluated in a standardised manner. The absence of a unified evaluation protocol hinders comparisons and progress in colorization research. In response, our study introduces the DFCI dataset, consisting of 10,000 high-quality, color-less and彩色 images in a standard dataset format, and utilizes the P3M metric, previously proposed in other studies, to assess the performance of various state-of-the-art colorization methods. The comprehensive evaluation using DFCI and P3M will offer an extensive evaluation of colorization methods and will facilitate future comparisons, leading to the creation of more effective colorization models.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on backpropagation. By applying the Merkle-Yang theorem, our method ensures the correct placement of decision trees within a multi-dimensional space. This approach leverages Newton-Cotes formulas to determine a subset of relevant features and utilizes a generalization of the mean value theorem for multiple variables. The method initially places a few random trees in regression spatial partitioning space and iteratively adds more trees based on the maximum prediction error until network capacity is reached. This approach can be directly applied to determine both the weights and structure of a fully connected, multi-layered ANN with multiple output nodes. By analyzing numerical results, our method showcases the neural network's ability to approximate complex target functions and generalizes well to novel, unseen data. This method is particularly advantageous in safety-critical applications, as it eliminates the need for backpropagation and provides fully interpretable multi-dimensional decision trees.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation.

A new type of line waves that can persist in both forward and backward directions and are confined to a space much larger than the size of the defining nanoantenna has been discovered. This phenomenon occurs at the boundary of two specially designed electromagnetic line arrays that have been crafted to consist of individual units.A demonstration of these line waves in visible light line sources is achieved through the use of optical tweezers, which leverage these line waves to guide the movement of particles. This strategy combines advanced light nanotechnology with visible light nanotechnology to achieve two outcomes: enhanced manipulation of particles and precision measurement of the direction of line waves.

One of the most promising approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is learning across multiple interacting agents, a concept widely recognized as a critical area of research in machine learning and cognitive robotics. This work delves into the potential of multi-agent learning methods for developing autonomous systems capable of solving complex real-world problems. It provides an in-depth analysis of multi-agent learning techniques applied in various domains and outlines key technological hurdles that need to be overcome. Furthermore, it identifies and discusses innovative solutions that allow this approach to effectively permeate diverse robotic application areas.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the medium regression model in a high-dimensional, imbalanced dataset. This estimator enables accurate parameter estimation by incorporating a innovative initial bias-corrected estimator. It was demonstrated to achieve the minimax optimal rate of estimation error when sparsity conditions are minimal. Furthermore, the bias-corrected estimator was shown to significantly reduce estimation error compared to the Lagrange Multiplicator (LM) estimator, particularly for large regression coefficients and under sparse sensitivity and sparsity conditions. This discovery was verified through numerical experiments, which showed the bias-corrected estimator outperformed traditional methods in terms of estimation error and medium-determined error.

The task of relation extraction is a crucial aspect of natural language understanding that captures important entity interactions. Currently, researchers have moved towards adopting a more standardized framework for this task by treating it as a classification problem. We examine various approaches to relation extraction as a classification task, focusing on different entity and relation representation techniques. We also explore the use of point-level, entity-level, and relation quantization strategies. Experiments conducted on the SemEval-2010 and SemEval-2014 datasets using multiple neural network architectures allow us to evaluate the effectiveness of these approaches and provide valuable insights for conducting efficient and accurate relation extraction operations.

The impact of anisotropy on the dissociation of quarkonium in N-dimensional space is investigated, generalizing the Glazkov Fiol model to account for temperature variations. This study finds that anisotropy and extra dimensions contribute to a lower dissociation temperature for quarkonia. Specifically, five-dimensional quarkonia and five-flavor mesons exhibit the most significant decrease in dissociation temperature.

Our study focused on the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7 using neutron diffraction, revealing a complex arrangement of its Ru1 and Ru2 atoms' moments, as well as its manganese ions, at lower temperatures. Contrary to earlier research, our findings suggest that a significant portion of the ru moments are ordered, not frozen, and that the molecular arrangement of its manganese ions is also ordered below 15K. Furthermore, the distribution of its ru atoms into two distinct sites appears to be independent of the magnetic properties within the system.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons have become highly effective in learning the underlying patterns within data, yet their direct application as a signal representation for images and videos is limited due to the substantial memory demands imposed by their parameterization. In response, we introduce a novel dual-MLP architecture that effectively supplants traditional images and videos, enabling efficient encoding and decoding of signals through a pair of interconnected networks. One network, the encoder, maps a signal to a set of discrete points in latent space, while its paired decoder maps these points back to the signal, with an emphasis on minimizing the discrepancy. Our proposed method exhibits significant memory efficiency gains of up to 4 times when compared to existing approaches for high-resolution image and video encoding and decoding.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data to adjust model parameters according to a predetermined distribution assumption, yet these approaches can be susceptible to inaccuracies in parameters and potentially suboptimal performance due to the presence of noise and anomalies. Drawing inspiration from semi-supervised learning methods which effectively utilize unlabelled data to refine parameters and accelerate convergence, we propose a novel technique that integrates adaptation and semi-supervised learning to improve generalization in unsupervised classification tasks. This technique leverages a weighted semi-supervised entropy minimization method that accounts for the distribution of unlabelled samples within each class, taking into consideration their density, to correct model parameters and accelerate convergence accordingly. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared to existing weighted methods and baseline models.

Despite its overwhelming success, the geometric architecture of complex deep learning systems remains poorly understood. By categorizing different deep learning systems into geometric structures, we can analyze their internal workings more effectively, ultimately paving the way for developing new learning algorithms with robust theoretical foundations, including those for attention mechanisms and batch normalization, and leading to discoveries in geometric group theory and non-commutative geometry, which in turn may inspire innovations in quantum machine learning.

We consider the field extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ formed by adjoining the $2n$-th roots of unity to the rationals. Our approach combines algebraic and analytic techniques to determine which ambiguous principal ideals have generators that are invariant under the Galois group of $K/\mathbb{Q}$. A novel method is introduced to establish the asymptotic count of such generators, ultimately allowing us to prove that not all ambiguous principal ideals are generated by elements that are inert in $K/\mathbb{Q}$. This result resolves an issue first posed by Fr\"{o}hlich in the early 1970s.

A novel method is introduced to enhance the performance of deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques by integrating external variables, drawn from a pre-defined set of established techniques called substructure variables. The variability in these variables is quantified and incorporated into the classification model as 'one-hot encoding' features, allowing the network access to varying levels of variability within the variables. This can be likened to providing the network with an understanding of traditional substructure variables and their inherent variability. The technique is tested on a demonstrator network for two-pronged resubstructure tagging, yielding improved classification accuracy in simulation. Additionally, techniques from this method may also be beneficial to other deep neural network applications in jet substructure tagging.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, and we derive formulas to calculate them. Additionally, we provide a corresponding formula for numbers similar to these Stirling numbers but tailored for combinations rather than partitions.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties were calculated symbolically, taking advantage of fast computation of rotation matrices between equivalent points and their interplanar spacings. The efficiency of this computation was attributed to a fast algorithm for determining the action of point groups on coordinates and an easily accessible set of transformation matrices.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories of constant curvature. Specifically, they can be classified as compact types with a consistent curvature, which includes spheres, Euclidean spaces, and cosets of compact and discrete types from spheres and hyperbolic spaces. Furthermore, it's demonstrated that for non-flat, simply connected manifolds of constant positive curvature, Killing vector fields exist only under specific linear transformations. Consequently, such momentum operators can be defined only under specific transformations, which can be represented using real numbers, integers, or Fibonacci numbers, respectively.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces additional complex phases that arise from the Jacobian determinant, and the severity of the sign problem depends on both the original and new formulations. We compare the performance of the sign problem across multiple many-body wave function representations, including the single-particle, Slater determinant, and Gaussian ansatz, and demonstrate that the transformed simulation exhibits a significantly reduced severe sign problem, with an average statistical error reduction of two orders of magnitude for a system in the excited state.

In a composite Higgs model, the expected $Z'$ boson is accompanied by a complex scalar field that acts as a $U(1)_Y$ gauge symmetry's "matter candidate." The $U(1)_Y$ gauge boson is produced when this field condenses, though it had been assumed that its mass is generated through the standard mechanism. We now propose a new method for a $z$-boson decay into these scalar fields, which results in distinct yet testable signatures at the LHC, including large missing transverse energy and isolated leptons or photons.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, enabling users to traverse farther distances within a VR environment than they could step in place. Nevertheless, current approaches to VR perception manipulation, such as haptic devices and walking in place, can often be uncomfortable for users to use. This paper summarizes our VR research, highlighting the universal challenges and opportunities for innovative designs that can adapt a user's perception more comfortably. Through VR perception manipulation, we aim to comfortably expand users' VR experiences beyond their physical constraints, ultimately allowing them to walk further and VR systems to render environments larger than what a user's step distance and room size allow for.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations of low-mass star formation have been conducted
using the VLA, ALMA, and NOEMA. These studies have been published in observations of
OFC-437 and ALMA-2017-1. The ALMA and NOEMA data have been used to simulate the binary
formation process in a 30 $M_{\odot}$ parent core using a code called Collapsing. The
mass of the parent core is not as high as is typical, and the binary formation is being
studied in a scenario that ends in disc fragmentation. 

The mass of each fragment is influenced by the total mass of the parent core. As the
total core mass decreases, the mass of each fragment becomes more similar. 

The distribution of binary mass ratios in the simulations is not the same as in other
studies of low-mass star formation. This is because, in those studies, the cores were
much less massive, at about 1 $M_{\odot}$. As a result, the distribution of binary mass
ratios is different. 

The mass distribution of binaries in the same region can be studied in detail. Most binaries
have a total mass of about 20 $M_{\odot}$. This is similar to the mass of the parent core,
and it suggests that binary formation is more efficient at forming high-mass stars.
