A specific application of this model, where dependent variables share a common structure, is explored. Estimators for model parameters are developed using modified likelihood functions and these are applied to estimate extreme weather events using wind and ocean data from the North East Atlantic between 2003 and 2018 are used wind speed and significant wave height measurements are used.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human-like motion preferences and aids in teaching robots this preference. However, current methods have a limitation, as they only permit static adjustments to a robot's environment, such as modifying human height or base tool position, leading to suboptimal results in complex tasks. We've developed a framework to model preferences dynamically, enabling teaching of a wide range of robot behaviors including posture and hand or arm movements. By incorporating this model into a control law, a smooth and efficient robot motion emerges, with the teaching input's magnitude and direction having meaningful effects on observed behavior, even in situations with position and velocity restrictions.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\text{HH}\rightarrow \text{b}\bar{\text{b}}\text{W}\text{W}\rightarrow \lambda_{\text{F}}\bar{\text{b}}\text{W}\text{V}$ final state at both the LHC and HL-LHC, we apply a new, efficient method for calculating next-to-leading order standard model cross sections using $\Phi$-space slicing. This framework simplifies complex calculations by redefining phase space variables. The computed results are validated against known next-to-leading order standard model and interference rates. We then assess the sensitivity of these measurements to effective field theory parameters within a simplified topological standard model extension, specifically its $\lambda_{\text{F}}\bar{\text{b}}$ and $\text{WV}$ components. These coefficients control the $\text{H}\rightarrow \text{b}\bar{\text{b}}$ and $\text{W}\text{V}$ interaction strengths. Our analysis indicates that the $\text{W}\rightarrow \text{b}\bar{\text{b}}}$ coupling can be measured with a precision of $\sim 10\%$, while the $\text{W}\text{V}$ coupling can be measured with a precision of $\sim 5\%$.

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models using in-the-wild videos, which are characterized by diverse classes, backgrounds, and transformations such as rotations, occlusions, and distortions. This unique dataset offers unprecedented variety and variety in real-world scenarios, significantly outperforming traditional data sources in the field. The proposed method leverages a 3D bounding box hypothesis generation approach, a novel single-view 3D pose estimation algorithm, and a 3D pose refinement technique utilizing dense pixel-wise cost maps. The developed method, 6PoseInW, was trained on a large, diverse dataset consisting of a million YouTube videos featuring over 750 classes of objects. The results demonstrate the superiority of 6PoseInW over state-of-the-art models, particularly in the field of 3D pose estimation, while achieving impressive 3D pose accuracy of a mean 3D pose error (P3D) of 0.204 on the KITTI dataset without any fine-tuning. The source code for 6PoseInW is publicly available at https://github.com/6PoseInW/6PoseInW.

Our comprehension of how people process, use, and disseminate misinformation is limited due to the fragmented nature of the available data. This lack of understanding hinders the effectiveness of information campaigns aimed at reducing the rejection of COVID-19 vaccines. By utilizing a comprehensive approach that involves extracting and linking multiple knowledge sources, we have created the MisinfoMap: the first comprehensive knowledge graph centered on COVID-19 vaccine misinformation. This knowledge base allows us to explore the various knowledge graphs that contribute to our current knowledge of vaccine misinformation and to analyze how people make decisions regarding the issue, such as whether to accept or reject the vaccines, based on the information they encounter. This approach enables us to identify and visualize the information sources that influence people's behavior, as well as the myths and factual evidence associated with them. Furthermore, our analysis of the knowledge graph's structure reveals the characteristics of the current knowledge base, including the information that supports people's decisions regarding the vaccines, as well as the associated fears, such as those related to cancer and blood disorders.

Advancements in attosecond science for characterizing electron dynamics can be accelerated by producing higher-order harmonic sources with greater energy and repetition rates. We propose a method combining waveguide technology and carrier-envelope phase phase-locking to achieve this. This approach enables us to experimentally verify a conversion efficiency of 0.65% from infrared power to attosecond pulse yield, establishing a record. This breakthrough could enable direct absorption imaging of single electrons.

Researchers have discovered two periodic changes in the eclipse times of the eclipsing binary AI Men, with a 104-day period causing an acceleration and a 307-day period causing an acceleration four times larger. The shorter period's change is likely due to the asymmetry in the binary system, while the longer period's effect is best explained by a complex and potentially chaotic apsidal motion. The case of AI Men highlights that a simple and regular pattern in eclipse times may not always be present, emphasizing the need for comprehensive data analysis.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under conditions of focusing nonlinearity with masses exceeding the critical threshold and negative total energy. We demonstrate that solutions in this scenario are uniformly bounded and that their $L^2$-norm does not grow indefinitely over time. Building upon a prior work of the authors, which established that solutions become weakly asymptotic to a stationary state, we now prove that solutions become strongly asymptotic to the same state.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations by incorporating mathematical constraints into a flexible and adaptable framework.  Despite their versatility in handling diverse initial and boundary conditions, they often struggle with efficiency when solving complex initial-boundary value problems.  We have developed an enhanced version of these networks, which can accelerate solving such problems, by initially approximating the solution using traditional numerical methods and training the model to match that result.  Training is confined to areas where the solution requires refinement, and we have found this approach to be effective across a broad range of examples, with significant improvements in training time.

This study examines the behavior of ferroelectric field-effect transistors with the positive-ferroelectric phase. We analyze how the capacitance of these transistors changes in response to various factors, including electric field, gate voltage, and position within the device. Our investigation focuses on the dynamic behavior of these transistors, which we model using a circuit with a gate, oxide, and ferroelectric layers. By solving the equations governing the system, we calculate the time-dependent transfer charge and compare our results to experiments, thus validating the model. We also explore the effects of negative capacitance on the transistor's operation and find that it can lead to an increase in the slope factor below one, a desirable characteristic for low-power devices. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic behavior of transistors with unfavored ferroelectric phase, which has been largely overlooked in previous studies.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's security architecture, particularly concerning prevalent security threats and their potential impacts on ecosystem integrity. To address this knowledge shortfall, we conducted an in-depth vulnerability analysis of Cargo's core components, including Rust, crates.io, and cargo itself. By manually inspecting historical data, we discovered 240 previously unknown security vulnerabilities across these components, with security research showing that Cargo's ecosystem is susceptible to six distinct attack vectors. As a result, we proposed ten remedial measures to mitigate these risks and further discovered that cargo and Rust each contain a previously unknown vulnerability.

For analyzing typical behavior in irreducible stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to confirm the non-singularity of the associated probability measure with respect to a specific condition. This study leverages a well-established result by Lasota and Nowicki's framework to establish the absolute continuity of the probability measure for quasi-isometric STT systems with stochastic perturbations. Moreover, it leverages this finding to demonstrate the typicality of non-singular measures for stochastic STT systems beyond the constraints of non-singular conditions.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This parameter is linked to the group's p-Sylow subgroups, where the minimum degree corresponds to $p^2-3$ under certain conditions, and $4$ otherwise. Furthermore, we've established that the power graph's vertices can be covered by $m(G)$ disjoint cycles, where $m(G)$ is this minimal degree divided by $3$. This is equivalent to identifying $m(G)$ elements that generate G's maximal cyclic subgroups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (0.1 < |x_F| < 0.5) have not been extensively explored at higher energy levels. The ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC has collected data from p-Pb collisions occurring at 5.02 TeV, paired with fixed-target 16O-Ne collisions at 100 A GeV, to investigate charged hadron production patterns across the full rapidity range and transverse momentum region (2 < p_T < 100 GeV/c and 0.3 < x_F < 0.9). The observed results for both charged hadron yields and transverse momenta demonstrate significant scaling consistency, suggesting a scalable relationship based on nuclear collision dimensions.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image recognition models, but they require extensive pre-processing and parameter tuning to minimize noise in the input data. This often leads to excessive data refinement that can distort image features and reduce their clarity. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach by replacing pixel-wise operations with orientation-based convolutions, allowing the construction of Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs). These networks can effectively learn features from orientation-sensitive elementary images and are insensitive to geometric noise, thus eliminating the need for extensive pre-processing. We demonstrate the efficacy of OCNs on several benchmark datasets, including MNIST and ORCO-2, and show how they can be optimized for better performance.

This study focuses on enhancing the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We examine how GCNs are applied to point clouds and the resulting optimization possibilities. By tightening the definition of graph convolution, we can select an optimal network size for a given task while maintaining a balanced distribution of operations. This allows us to apply a gradient-based method to fine-tune GCN parameters and achieve a customized, efficiently structured model. We evaluate our approach on various benchmarks, including semantic segmentation and geometric prediction, and achieve notable reductions in computational costs with little impact on performance.

We introduce a new type of host-based Trojan attack, using non-functional triggers that do not harm the system, allowing security analysts to be deceived into thinking the malware is benign. This approach is innovative because it employs trigger obfuscation through code fragmentation and a custom interpreter, making it resilient against static analysis techniques. The effectiveness of this attack can be enhanced by making triggers adaptable to various environments, making it an attractive option for triggering Trojan stages via compromised applications. We've developed a flexible and adaptable loader that can be triggered by non-functional triggers, making it an effective method for deploying malicious code.

We are developing an imaging spectrograph known as ROSIE IFU, which will be integrated into the Very Large Telescope's Extremely Wide Angle and Spectroscopy Investigator Tool instrument suite. Each of our spectrograph's cameras contains a unique lens that captures a distinct point in the sky's two-dimensional space. These lenses are arranged in a grid pattern to capture a targeted area of the sky. Inside each lens, a grating with 600 lines per millimeter breaks down light into specific wavelengths with high precision. This allows us to analyze the composition of celestial objects. We have designed a set of lenses that cover a broad area of the sky, which we refer to as the 'Pupil array'. This pupil array consists of over 200 individually shaped lenses that cover a 10 arcminute by 10 arcminute area of the sky. This array is split into multiple sections that correspond to different wavelength ranges. We have implemented a series of filters to separate these sections, which allow us to accurately measure the composition of celestial objects. This breaks down light into specific wavelengths with high precision, which we refer to as 'spectra'. We have designed a set of filters that separate these spectra into different sections of the 'Pupil array', which contain over 200 individually shaped lenses that cover a 10 arcminute by 10 arcminute area of the sky. In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck et al. (Eur. Phys. J. A50, 67 (2014)) are considered in light of progress made since then. The revisiting highlights the relevance of new double beta decay measurements, a significant number of doublet and triplet 2+ states discovered through isobaric multiplet mass relationships, and recently calculated two-proton radioactivity data. These new data have led to notable conclusions including a substantial enhancement of two-proton radioactivity in certain nuclei and refined two-proton radioactivity predictions, as well as enhanced two-proton radioactivity in certain nuclei and refined two-proton radioactivity predictions, as well as enhanced two-proton radioactivity in certain nuclei.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system variations and environmental changes, leading to distorted CSI and impaired localization. This research introduces a novel DNN architecture that leverages learned representations from a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) to capture robust features from raw CSI. By incorporating these features, the proposed end-to-end DNN achieves superior localization performance in both controlled settings (indoor) and real-world scenarios. The efficacy of this approach has been validated through extensive experiments utilizing the 802.11 WiFi protocol, yielding impressive results.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this assumption was disproven. This work extends the Strong Edge Coloring problem into three dimensions, proposing analogs of previously conjectured properties and testing them on a cube-based graph, 1 3 -coloring a 3-dimensional grid with a  2  2  2 subgraph constraint and $\mathbb{L}_3$-coloring a  3  3  3 grid with a -claw constraint.

We investigate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Hamming graphs H_n(2) and H_n(3), confirming conjectures put forth by Coven and Linderman. The eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix A for H_n(q) were initially determined by Biggs, whose eigenspaces remained enigmatic until now. A general method to compute a basis for each eigenspace D_{i,n}(λ_i) of H_n(q) is presented, specifically for q=2 and q=3. The eigenvalue λ_i has multiplicity (choose(n, i))(λ_i - q + 1 - 1) in H_n(q). The eigenbasis for H_2(3) and H_3(3) is particularly established.

COPASI is a widely-used application for analyzing time-dependent network models in areas like biochemical and genetic networks. The model functions as a singleton, with users interacting through the CopasiWScript. To enhance accessibility for R users and pre-COPASI model sharing, the CopasiWScript ShinyCOPASI was created, enabling visualization and analysis of CopASI models within web browsers, with the feature of integrating seamlessly with RStudio.

Deep neural networks have become the preferred method for data-driven inference, but they are not foolproof due to various factors, such as model selection and training, which can introduce classification and prediction uncertainties. While current methods often overlook uncertainty in the output values, this can lead to unreliable predictions and inaccurate confidence levels. In this research, a novel approach is proposed to quantify uncertainties associated to neural network-based inference, which includes uncertainties in class probabilities and predictions for both supervised classification and unsupervised feature extraction tasks. The method leverages conformal prediction for generating confidence intervals and entropy-based uncertainty for predicting output features. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets in both regression and classification contexts.

This research quantum group analogue of the work by Galindo and Suzuki, which examined quasi-split inclusions of surface singularities from geometric perspective. We were able to expand their findings to include reduced cross-sectional slices of quantum surface singularities, which are defined by a quantum parameter.

We introduce an extended version of the actor-critic algorithm for policy evaluation in large-scale Markov decision processes by incorporating a free probability theory. This represents the first application of stochastic step-size gradient descent in prior research. Leveraging semi-circular and Wigner distribution properties, we derive a first-order asymptotic expansion that yields a significant simplification. As a result, our method can efficiently evaluate policies for large-state MDPs. Empirical tests on control tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves precise value function estimates, and we provide theoretical and practical insights into the selection of the step-size parameter.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line graphs are equivalent.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem associated with hydrological measurements of rainfall and runoff at a specific location, by applying a computer simulator of runoff based on the physically-distributed SHY model. By utilizing the simulator and an algorithm of global optimization, it is possible to reconstruct rainfall time series from runoff time series or vice versa. When imperviousness of the terrain is taken into consideration, there are distinct approaches to simulate rainfall or reconstruct missing data time series, each tailored to specific scenarios. These methods are illustrated through real-world examples drawn from hydrological monitoring stations in Croatia.

Research has shown that certain leadership queries can help build learning models which are resistant to distributional shifts.  In this context, we focus on a specific type of query known as local membership queries (LMQs), where each query corresponds to a local area in the data space.  Our work demonstrates two main outcomes: (a) it is possible to accurately learn a distribution shift detection model using a small number of LMQs, and our model achieves optimal performance in semi-supervised learning with Lipschitz loss functions, and (b we successfully create an effective model for robust classification using only LMQs, and our results exceed those of several contemporary methods even in scenarios with ample labeled data, while also yielding theoretical guarantees).  Our experiments show that our proposed method is particularly resilient to situations with limited labeled data, resulting in improved accuracy on clean and adversarial samples, compared to leading leadership-based approaches known to produce classification models which are known susceptible to such queries.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with multiple particles have been measured in both proton-proton and lead-lead collisions using the ATLAS detector at the LHC. This analysis involves selecting 60-80 GeV c-level jets and calculating their associated particles within specific radial and rapidity ranges in the perpendicular direction. Key characteristics of jet-associated particles are examined across different collision types, including centrality, and considering various radial and rapidity ranges. Relative to proton-proton collisions, a decrease of 10-20% is observed in the fragmentation function of central lead-lead collisions. This is observed within the radius range of 0.2 to 0.4, and a similar trend is observed at larger radii with a decrease of approximately 15% for R=0.3. A decrease of 10-15% is observed in the leading particle's transverse momentum distribution in central lead-lead collisions compared to proton-proton collisions. These results are consistent with simulations that model jet energy loss.

Recent research involving Apéry-type binomial series has led to numerous nontrivial series evaluations being transformed into a specific type of representation known as multiple binomial series. This study aims to develop a new class of representation for high-order central binomial inverse values using the format of multiple infinite series.

The discovery of Y dwarfs has led to significant interest in brown dwarf classification. Recent research has led to the identification of potential Y dwarfs in the SDSS data archives. A new, more robust approach is proposed in this article to confirm these discoveries by utilizing near-infrared photometry from the Wide Field Camera on the Submillimeter-BOSSON board. This method is more resistant to systematic biases and is particularly effective in detecting Y dwarfs with distinct red-to-infrared color patterns. A database of low-mass stars has been compiled to validate the proposed color-based selection criteria. This database is accessible to the scientific community to facilitate further Y dwarf searches.

A significant finding in high-energy collisions revealed by ALICE at LHC is the influence of the radial flow on the p_T distributions of baryons and mesons, which also depends on the charged-particle multiplicity. This correlation can be explained by the fact that heavier ions produce a more compact, hotter collision zone, resulting in increased radial flow and higher charged-particle multiplicity. Furthermore, the similarity in light-flavour baryon to meson ratios across different systems indicates that light-flavour quarkonia may exhibit a similar pattern, potentially offering insight into the quenching of heavy-flavour quarkonia in a quark-gluon plasma.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching.

Experimental 3D printing of Martian and Lunar regolith simulants using a Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) technique was conducted with modifications to accommodate their distinct properties. These changes include heating the build chamber, using a heated bed, and adapting pre-treatment processes to account for differing vapor pressures. A Gallium-assisted size reduction treatment known as GARR was implemented to assess its effectiveness in preparing simulant materials for FFF printing. Moreover, we investigated methods to improve material performance through the addition of water, heat, binding agents, and compression, aiming to optimize the mechanical properties of printed materials. A key finding is that direct Fused Filament Fabrication of Martian and Lunar simulant materials using (FFS) is not feasible under current conditions, likely due to polymer degradation caused by excessive heating. Nevertheless, a combination of extrusion and compression has proven effective in producing samples with sufficient compressive strength at a temperature well below the thermal limits for PCL, allowing for potential construction of real-world planetary materials.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to analyze a film on a fiber with a specific surface energy pattern. The resulting model reveals that a higher contact angle leads to faster growth of disturbances in the liquid film. Moreover, a transition from stable to unstable behavior occurs at a threshold wavelength, which varies with liquid-solid slip. Interestingly, this slip effect can influence a film's stability in ways similar to gravity or surface tension.

By comparing the Brackett-$\alpha$, gamma, and delta lines with SBCS20's photometric Star Formation Rate measurements at $z \approx 6.5$, we found discrepancies of up to a factor of 200 in Star Formation Rate measurements derived from these lines. SBCS20 concluded that the Br$\gamma$ line is a more reliable indicator of SFR than Br$\alpha$. Our comparison of Br$\gamma$ and Br$\alpha$ measurements indicates a moderate dust extinction ($A_{\rm Br\gamma} \approx 0.1$), aligning with expectations for star-forming galaxies. We suggest that variability in the Br$\gamma$ to Br$\alpha$ ratio, potentially caused by star formation, could account for the observed discrepancies in SFR measurements. Our findings demonstrate that Br$\gamma$ line measurements are suitable for Br$\alpha$ SFR measurements, though Br$\delta$ measurements exhibit variability potentially due to variability in the ionizing spectrum. Our data reveal a greater variability in the Br$\delta$ to Br$\gamma$ ratio than in the Br$\gamma$ to Brackett beta (Br$\beta$) ratio, indicating a stronger ionization-dependent variability in the former. Our data also confirm a positive correlation between the Br$\delta$ to Br$\gamma$ line ratio and the [O III] 88$\mu$m / [N II] 57$\mu$m diagnostic diagram, where galaxies

This paper completes the classification of the braided auto-equivalences of local modules over the SU(2) level Kac Moore vertex operator algebra for specific exceptional orbifolds. It also identifies four exceptional orbifles as SU(2) level 1, 2, 4, and 6 under the condition that the local module category possesses non-degenerate braided auto-equivalences. With this addition, we achieve a complete classification of simple modular categories derived from SU(2) level $k \neq 0$ that contain only invertible objects. Furthermore, for levels $k \neq 0$, we find that the only auto-equivalences of the local modules category are the orbifolding categories of SU(2) level $k$ for su(2) at levels $1, 2, 4, 6$.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher in 1937 to describe the spread of a beneficial allele within a population. This equation can be reformulated into an abstract Cauchy problem in a Banach space setting. Our main contribution lies in demonstrating the existence of a mild solution to this Cauchy problem, achieved by establishing a semigroup of operators through a probabilistic approach related to the branching process of independent random walks with an infinitesimal generator belonging to the Levy-Khintchine class. Additionally, our work examines the long-term behavior of the mild solution, specifically the asymptotic profile of the branching random walk as time progresses.

This study addresses the challenge of handwritten mathematical term classification. A novel method is proposed to identify whether a handwritten input is part of the training set or not. It then uses this binary classifier in conjunction with multiple handwritten character recognition systems to perform open-vocabulary classification of mathematical expressions. To accomplish this, the input is first segmented into its character segment features and subsequently fed to each recognition system. The output hand-written character is used in combination with the segment features to determine if the input is part of the training set or not. To evaluate the effectiveness of this method, the recognition rate is computed for both binary and multi-class classification tasks. The results of the single letter recognition systems and the overall method are then presented.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modeling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by integrating a hidden Markov model (HMM) with a non-paramedian distribution. The proposed approach minimizes the difference between predicted and actual durations, ultimately aiming to generate more natural-sounding speech. Notably, this method can be applied seamlessly to any duration model that produces a predicted distribution for the random variable of interest. The benefits of this approach are confirmed through synthesis tests, which show improved naturalness and intelligibility of the synthesized speech. The speech synthesis system with the median-based duration modeling outperforms its mean-based counterpart in terms of overall quality and naturalness.

Species distribution models are a fundamental aspect of species conservation strategies. They are typically developed using statistical methods that incorporate occurrence records and various environmental and spatial covariates. This work presents a Bayesian estimation of ten bird species in the island of Madeira, utilizing ten covariates derived from both natural and human-related sources. The analysis is based on occurrence records from natural observations, expert opinions, and banding studies. To address uncertainty in the data, an expert-driven approach is used to consider multiple natural observation sources, which leads to a comprehensive species distribution estimation. The results highlight how bias and uncertainty in the estimates fluctuate across the island, with a notably lower rate in urban areas. This study also provides a detailed map of each species' distribution and the associated estimation uncertainty. The approach presented can be applied generally, underscoring the significance of considering uncertainty and all available data when assessing species' habitats and conservation needs.

Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long wait times for dermatology appointments. Moreover, the shortage of pathologists and limited access to medical specialists result in subpar skin cancer diagnosis and treatment. To overcome these challenges, a collaborative deep learning approach between computer scientists and dermatologists was proposed. This model, trained on a large dataset of dermatology images, was then fine-tuned by experienced dermatologists on this dataset. The collaboration yielded positive outcomes, as evidenced by a study published in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology in 2019. The authors highlight that interactive deep learning holds significant potential for widespread adoption in medical imaging, particularly in skin lesion analysis.

To identify the essential characteristics of Type Ia supernovae from spectral data, we applied a probabilistic autoencoder with physically-grounded parameters to a set of 1112 supernovae observed in the San Diego Supernova Project database. By incorporating a Kippenhahn-Dieterich model, we established a connection between spectral spectra and the autoencoder's latent space. Our findings reveal that the autoencoder learns a representation of radial velocity dispersion, which is closely associated with pre-explosion binary interactions. Furthermore, this new representation can enhance our comprehension of how binary interactions impact supernovae and the potential to distinguish between supernovae resulting from different binary systems.

A massive neutral gas outflow was observed in a heavy star-forming galaxy. The outflow was found to be moving away at 19,000 km/s, and its extended CO emission and dust star formation suggest it originates from a region of active star formation. The outflow has an immense atomic gas mass of 1.66 x 10^10 solar masses. This outflow has a mass outflow rate of 1.66 x 10^2 solar masses per year when averaged over a 10 million year timescale. The energy required to create this outflow is approximately 4.5 x 10^10 solar masses per year. The energy from massive star formation in this galaxy is insufficient to account for the outflow's creation, and it appears that outflows may be a common feature of heavy star-forming galaxies.

In a laboratory setting, researchers studied the movement of fluid and heavy particles in a steady, symmetric plume that moves upward and moved into different density environments with varying fluid and particle fluxes. By controlling how fluid and particles entered and exited the plume, they examined how this affected the surrounding fluid. The results showed that when particles were entering the plume, they slowed its growth. The reduction in fluid within the plume and plume decreased significantly. The analysis also found that particle interactions within the plume and reduced turbulence caused by these particles. Conversely, when particles were leaving the plume, they accelerated its growth by increasing the plume and by an average of for a range of ratios. Theoretical models and simulations using a two-phase plume confirmed these findings.

Understanding the spread of diseases within networks of individuals in contact has been a long-standing goal. By mapping disease data to graphs of patient connections, researchers have sought to trace and understand epidemics. Traditional contact graphs, however, assume that all individuals within a location interact equally, which is often not the case in reality. Certain individuals may have more frequent or prolonged contact with others, increasing their likelihood of transmitting the disease. To better capture these nuances, we propose representing disease spread as a hypergraph, where triplets of individuals who interact are used to model non-uniform transmission risks. This approach enables us to theorize and measure how non-uniform transmission affects different distance metrics in disease graphs, ultimately shedding light on the visual characteristics of disease spread data. Empirically, our method reveals that disease spread data often exhibits a small-world structure, providing valuable insights for public health officials to make informed decisions.

Recently, it was discovered that a layer-by-layer transition occurs in the properties of CrI$_3$ between its thick and thin film states, which raises curiosity about how its two-dimensional magnetic semiconducting behavior responds to external fields such as magnetic and electric ones. Our study reveals the influence of lattice distortions on magnetic and electric field responses using density functional theory, showing that spin canting effects are significantly reduced in 2D CrI$_3$ compared to its 3D counterpart. Observations indicate that a gap opening occurs in the single layer of CrI$_3$ due to ferromagnetic interactions when subjected to an in-plane electric field, while a magnetic field promotes ferromagnetism by generating a gap in the single layer of CrI3.

In solar-type stars, the rotation rate is influenced by the Rossby number. Our
investigation involved examining the rotation periods of over 80000 Gaia stars and
how the distribution of these rotation periods changes with the Rossby number.
Our results show a distinct break in the distribution at a specific Rossby number
value, indicating a shift from solid body rotation to differential rotation in solar-type
stars, as seen in solar observations. Additionally, the distribution of rotation
periods in solar-type stars deviates from models based on angular momentum conservation,
suggesting that the dynamic effects of the galactic environment impact the evolution
of stellar angular momentum.

A new deep model called K-fan structure has been developed to effectively process multiple inputs like text, images, and video. This structure uses a shared feature extraction layer that produces a multi-branch output, which is then combined using a shared fully-connected layer. The non-linear integration of modalities through this K-fan pattern enhances a model's ability to learn complex relationships between different input types, especially when the number of input classes is large. Furthermore, the K-fan pattern improves a model's ability to generalize by reducing overfitting, and it offers a scalable solution for feature integration as the number of input modalities increases. In our research, we applied the K-fan structure to a multi-modal single image annotation task, where it outperformed other models using significant margins of 10% to 15%.

The use of model checking as a method for verifying the correctness of concurrent programs has been demonstrated in previous studies. However, model checking alone is insufficient due to its focus on specified properties and the exclusion of external factors during program execution. In contrast, traditional unit and functional testing approaches, although limited in scope, can be adapted for testing concurrent programs by incorporating thread safety into code and data structures. Combining model checking and testing by using thread-safe data structures to eliminate basic concurrency issues and employing model checking to verify complex properties along with model checking-driven test generation may offer a practical and comprehensive strategy for ensuring the correctness of concurrent programs. The execution of model checking and testing in parallel may further enhance their efficiency. A key consideration in this process is the selection of an appropriate thread-safe library, which significantly influences the scope of verification and the cost of running the concurrent checker or test runner.

The widespread use of WhatsApp in everyday life in recent years has made it a crucial platform for both personal and professional communication. This has also facilitated the rapid dissemination of information and misinformation within closed user groups. Although the problem of misinformation exists on other online platforms, such as the internet and social media, the closed nature of WhatsApp groups allows a single user to reach a large number of people quickly and privately, posing a more significant issue that requires attention. Our proposed solution to tackle this problem is the MisinfoWhaATSAp system, an automated dataset and automated detection system for identifying misinformation in WhatsApp messages. This involves characterizing and collecting a large dataset of WhatsApp messages and visual media, as well as a machine learning model to classify them as misinformation or information. Our model shows promising results, achieving an accuracy rate of 90% in classifying misinformation, providing a solid foundation for further research and development in addressing the issue of misinformation on WhatsApp.

We examine a branching population where each individual's offspring distribution depends on the population's frequency spectrum. A frequency spectrum consists of distinct types or categories. As an example, in a binary case, we have individuals of different red and blue hues, with birth rates that depend on the proportion of each hue. Under certain conditions, we show that a frequency spectrum of at most n-1 is critical for obtaining limiting frequentcy. Furthermore, we present both examples and theoretical results illustrating that these results are optimal. These findings relate to problems of branching population and synchronization systems with nonlinear properties.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, adaptable activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our neural network. This enhanced AReLU is composed of two linear components and an attentiveness factor that is dynamically determined by the neural network. By optimizing these parameters, the AReLU allows our system to more effectively learn complex patterns and substantially enhance its accuracy compared to systems relying on standard linear activation functions.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model, offers a potential framework for understanding particle unification and dark matter but presents challenges in developing inflationary models due to potential threats to the delicate vacuum stability known as the de Sitter problem. Addressing this issue likely requires including supergravity's degree of freedom, which could introduce problematic couplings. We investigate the possibility of reconciling supergravity with inflation by exploring models where the scalar potential is entirely determined by a F-term, as proposed in super-F-term models. These models can be realized through coupling supersymmetric F-terms to a super-Weyl multiplet in four-dimensional N=1 supergravity. We analyze general super-F-term models within the T-dual framework of flux compactifications, which inherently satisfy this condition, providing potential solutions to the de Sitter problem. We derive a set of constraints resulting from F-term inflation in these models and demonstrate that an SU(2) gauge group is required to meet these constraints, implying that certain gauge symmetries are necessary to stabilize the vacuum in flux compactifications. We also outline necessary conditions for realizing such solutions through flux compactification.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and an equation was developed to show how the intensity of a laser's coherent population oscillations changes based on the direction of propagation. Conversely, the correlations of photon pairs created through down-conversion are not reciprocal. Specifically, the timing relationships between the pairs are correlated with the direction in which they travel.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as powerful platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs a novel technique to measure the electromagnetic interaction between photons and individual defects in superconducting quantum circuits. We utilize a quantum harmonic oscillator, programmed with Gattei's protocol, to amplify the response of distant charges, achieving coherent exchange of single photons. This amplification enables the exploration of non-linear interactions and crucially, it is adaptable to investigate various defects in real-time without altering the circuit design. Experimental findings confirm the protocol's efficacy and versatility.

We are looking for infinite cardinals $\kappa$ that allow for a division of the real number line $\mathbb{R}$ into $\lambda$ Borel sets, where each subset is homeomorphic to another, all of which are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. This research builds on Hausdorff work, initially showing that such a division is possible for $\aleph_1$ subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. Subsequent studies by Friedman, Kechris, Solecki, and Loewe established that cardinality is key in determining whether these divisions are possible. Our main discovery aligns with a hypothesis by Tarski, indicating that these divisions are only feasible when the number of subsets involved does not exceed the cardinality of the power set of the number line, allowing us to expand known results by Friedman et al.

This research examines whether established Commodity Trading Advisors can maintain their historical trading prowess after accounting for various market factors and a specific group of traders known for short-term reversal strategies. We identify a significant impact of these short-term reversal traders on CTAs with high historical success rates. Notably, their presence correlates with reduced CTA returns, lower alpha coefficients, and diminished profitability in subsequent years.

Identifying the application layer protocol is a crucial task for network security monitoring and surveillance. Nevertheless, accurately determining the protocol at this level is a challenging task for a variety of reasons. To tackle this issue, we suggest a novel approach for classifying the application using Bayesian theory, focusing on extracting relevant features such as packet count distribution and size distribution from each protocol. These features are then used to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experimental results obtained from commonly used application protocols.

Electrostatic gating allows for controlling the properties of materials, which makes it a powerful tool for doing so. A similar concept, the synergetic combination of light and synergetic interactions, has the potential to produce new and useful phenomena as well. We discovered this powerful combination in synergetic interactions of synergetic interactions of photons and magnons in a synergetic system consisting of a synergetic array of synergetic interactions. The system we studied is made up of synergetic interactions of photons and magnons in a synergetic array of synergetic interactions. By applying the rule of magnons and photons exchanging energy through interactions, we found that magnons could become efficient carriers of information. We also found that an electric field could control a synergetic phenomenon occurring in the system, resulting in a significant improvement in synergetic interactions. Our research has revealed a new rule of controlling synergetic phenomena through the rule of magnons and photons exchanging energy through interactions.

A new approach to federated learning is proposed for training deep models on a large number of devices that have non-identical data patterns. The method combines two key features: protecting the privacy of users and avoiding the centralized collection of user data. To address the issue of heterogeneous data patterns in a decentralized environment, the algorithm adopts a graph-based decentralized aggregation method that performs regular gradient averaging through periodic graph convolutions. The proposed graph is dynamically generated based on similarity in the input data and input class predictions to reduce the impact of heterogeneity. The algorithm is integrated with a input data-driven graph that is designed to be sparse and contains regular connections to minimize computational and communication costs. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated in experiments on synthetic and real-world data.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are employed. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink channel estimation in multi-user systems that utilize intelligent-reflecting-surface (IRS) assisted technology, which has gained significant attention for its ability to enhance wireless communication without increasing the infrastructure's scale. To tackle this complex issue, we have developed a novel approach that applies minimum-variance distortionless response (MVDR) principles to optimize an objective function derived from the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB). This iterative algorithm successfully identifies the precise location of the complex exponential terms within the objective function by leveraging special properties of Hermitian matrices and circumvents numerous local minima through a multi-stage candidate selection process that also considers the impact of noise. The results of our simulations confirm that this proposed estimation method achieves a lower CRLB compared to existing techniques.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Our analysis reveals that, initially, U.S. local news coverage closely mirrored national death rates, but this correlation diminished over time as regions with lower than expected case or death rates increased their coverage in response to national health updates and vaccine-related stories. Notably, urban areas with larger, better-educated, and politically progressive audiences tended to receive more information from non-partisan national and online sources, whereas rural areas gave more emphasis to local stations, whose coverage often downplayed the severity of the virus and promoted political agendas.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's a notable inflection point where children rapidly grasp and master numerical concepts between 8 and 18. We've approached this learning process from a machine learning perspective, where our experiments using supervised and self-supervised training methods revealed that the same inflection point emerges when introducing complex numerical properties. Furthermore, our techniques for teaching machines to count produced comparable results as those obtained through prior research, ultimately confirming that this inflection point is a inherent characteristic of counting ability.

Bloom filters offer quick assessment of whether an element belongs to a set, but they suffer from various types of errors in both positive and negative directions. To mitigate these issues, a new data structure, the Cuckoo Filter, has been developed, providing more stringent error constraints than Bloom filters, yet still enabling constant-time evaluations of set membership. However, implementing a Cuckoo Filter requires precise knowledge of the number of elements in a set, limiting its effectiveness when dealing with dynamic queries on mobile networks due to the overhead of extensive bitmaps and index tables required for implementation. To address this limitation, a new approach known as the Cuckoo Filter+ is proposed, allowing for dynamic queries on mobile networks by eliminating the need for a 64-bit index for each entry and significantly reducing storage requirements for unknown sets, thus facilitating efficient use within the constraints of mobile networks. This enhanced version of the Cuckoo Filter offers constant-time membership queries comparable to Bloom filters, but with substantially lower storage demands while providing zero false positives and a notable improvement in handling false negatives compared to existing Bloom filter enhancements. Furthermore, a new optimization technique has been created for mobile environments based on the Cuckoo Filter+, taking advantage of diverse hardware architectures in mobile devices by moving the computation of a hash function to the most suitable processor available on each device.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic functions on multi-linearity domains are explored in this paper. We demonstrate that any set of functions with a positive product in $\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{R}^n_+)^n$ can be used to derive an inequality of convex geometry nature through the pointwise inequality $|f_1(K,\dots,K)|\prod_{j=2}^n|f_j(L,\dots,L)|\leq|f_1(K,L,\dots,L)|\prod_{\substack{\textnormal{perm. of}\\
\textnormal{ positions of}\\
\textnormal{ $K$}}}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n|f_j(K,\dots,L,\dots,L)|$. In addition, any inequality of convex geometry nature can be translated into an inequality of holomorphic functions on polylinearity domains. We also establish a connection between the John ellipsoid and support functions, and extend an inequality related to the Brunn-Minkowski theorem to functions that are not necessarily homogeneous.

A new approach aims to derive market trend information from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, and how trading volumes converge as well. This methodology focuses on the dynamics of a single price equation, and how its solution provides a map from one price to another in a given time frame. By analyzing the divergence between prices in a single asset market, we can identify whether one price is superior to another in terms of being closer to the optimal price. This analysis is then applied to identify trends in both price and trading volume data from a single asset market, and how one price may be influenced by another in terms of being a speculative or fundamental price. Similarly, how future prices and trading volumes are analyzed to identify their relationships and how they converge in terms of being speculative or fundamental prices and how they are influenced by each other.

This paper presents FLVoogd, a refined method for training deep neural networks in a federated environment, safeguarding data from malicious attacks and privacy breaches within updates. Our approach uses local regularisation to prevent overfitting and reduce the effects of attacks, and applies DP-SGD to ensure privacy preservation of user updates. Furthermore, FLVoogd leverages the potential of over-parameterised models by using a pre-trained over-parameterised model as the global model, which enhances robustness and efficiency in learning. We demonstrate the efficacy of FLVoogd in several robust and private formulations, and empirical results show its robustness in predicting MNIST images under various attack scenarios.

We focus on developing a autonomous driving system that can learn the control strategy through observation. Our approach utilizes a simulation framework where the agent is only given input from the current scene, excluding any prior knowledge of the underlying physics. This is similar to training the system using data from a video game rather than the actual vehicle. We employ a hierarchical reinforcement learning model consisting of two neural networks, which we call the policy network and the critic network. The policy network generates control actions based on input state information and evaluates its decisions by estimating their future benefits. The critic validation takes place at an actual vehicle, where data is collected to update the critic's estimates. We employ a hybrid offline and online learning technique to efficiently update the critic using an extensive dataset, and then perform localized search after each update to improve the policy's decisions. We evaluate the resulting control strategies using a simulation framework with various driving scenarios and compare their safety levels to those achieved by other state-of-the-art strategies.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos. Furthermore, it proposes future research directions for tackling deepfake-related issues.

The discovery and characterization of sub-Neptune sized exoplanets orbiting within the habitable zones of their host stars have raised questions regarding the internal evolution of these planets and whether they could support habitable oceans on their surfaces. This study, focused on sub-Neptune sized exoplanets orbitting M-dwarf stars, investigates how various factors such as stellar XUV radiation and core composition influence the evolution of these planets. It is revealed that for planets with low levels of core volatiles, located in the habitable zones of their stars, a major atmosphere loss event occurs during their early evolution, resulting in the near total loss of their envelopes and the creation of rocky planets with potential surface oceans in the habitable zones, potentially supporting habitable oceans. In contrast, for planets with high levels of core volatiles, multiple scenarios of core and envelope evolution are possible, with the final configurations of these planets dependent on the initial core volatile content. These water-rich planets, with potential surface oceans in the habitable zones, could be suitable candidates for further investigation. It is concluded that the core composition is a crucial factor in the final core mass and the presence of potential habitable oceans on these planets, and that further research into how the core volatile content affects the core and envelope mass of these planets, as well as the core composition and the core and envelope mass through photoevaporation and core erosion, could be essential in the final core mass and the presence of potential habitable oceans on

This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that a sequence of 2:1 binary neuron connections can be trained via spike-timing dependent plasticity to learn a temporal sequence of patterns, even without predefined asymmetric connections. Through a combination of mathematical analysis and computer simulations, we found that the network can be spontaneously generated to hold the necessary memory for pattern recognition and that the learned patterns can be cycled in a temporal sequence, consistent with the predictions of a theoretical model. Our results suggest that simple binary connections can be sufficient for the learning of temporal patterns and that the source of asymmetry in connections can emerge from a common input without the need for specialized circuit design.

This paper presents an approach to improve the accuracy of scene text OCR models by leveraging multi-scale character representations. Existing OCR models are not well-equipped to handle text variations they haven't encountered during training. To address this limitation, our method replicates the character ocr2000 model on the ICD2019 dataset and compares it with the standard Keras OCR model. Our model achieves higher accuracy on the ICD2019 test set and maintains comparable performance on other benchmarks.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking of deterministic systems under random perturbations, which can be applied to validate chaos expansions for steady-states as well. Examples are included to demonstrate the proposed methodology.

In industrial settings, monitoring complex high-dimensional data is crucial. Nonetheless, dealing with high-dimensional data comes with several challenges, including data analysis difficulties and storage limitations. To address these issues, numerous techniques have been developed to simplify the data and identify the most critical variables, but they have significant drawbacks. To mitigate these problems, we developed a novel approach that employs a new optimization criterion and yigal volovich's special properties to create an effective method for concurrent data reduction and variable selection in semi-supervised partial least discriminant analysis. This method is particularly valuable in the quality and process monitoring of high-dimensional data. To demonstrate its efficacy, we applied it to a real-world case study and compared it with other existing methods on both a cement plant dataset and a blood transfusion dataset, analyzing the results with several performance metrics. The experimental results show that our proposed method outperforms traditional fully-supervised partial least discriminant analysis methods and data pre-processing methods in terms of accuracy and storage efficiency.

Using detailed orbital analysis based on precise star orbit data, we have created and refined a cluster of likely accreted dwarf galaxy remnants. By applying a sophisticated analytical technique, we've created robust, overlapping mass models that effectively capture the spatial and orbital characteristics of three distinct peaks. Our three-inflection e-folding timescales indicate that the accreted Gaia-Sausage Encelagous and Wukong/LMS-1 dwarf galaxies were accreted approximately 10-12 billion and 4.5-6 billion years ago respectively. Our analysis further suggests the presence of encelagous debris with retrograde orbits that may originate from a previously accreted dwarf galaxy with similar characteristics. Our models' masses are comparable to those predicted by previous analysis, and our analysis is relatively insensitive to the specific mass models used. Our comparative analysis reveals that the accreted Segue 1 and LMC1 galaxies share similar characteristics with the GSE and WUK deformities, whereas accreted Carina and LMC galaxies show minimal similarities to any deformity in the outer galactic plane respectively

For a finitely presented profinite group G, a finitely generated S[[G]]-module M, and a prime p with G having cohomological p-dimension at most 2, we establish that M's homotopy orbit spectral sequence converges strongly to a equivalent filtration-dgraded module where the p-power torsion in each degree stabilises. We deduce that M's continuous homology H_n(\G, M) has p-rank at most 1 for all n > 0. We verify this rank one property in specific instances by calculating the continuous homology of the Iwasava module S[[\G]]/\langle f\rangle, given that its Frel\G resolution is of length 2 and an Iwasava module's Frobenius endomorphism is denoted by f.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept" or "reject" options for partially created document sets. This is achieved by developing robust AI models that focus on minor document variations while maintaining accuracy, using a novel framework of selective label representation. Our experiments on document parsing tasks have shown that these models can match the performance of fully annotated counterparts by limiting the representation error to a 5% decline.

Previous studies on synthetic Eu/InAs bilayers with a metathesis reaction showed that Eu's conduction band minimum was lower than InAs's conduction band minimum, suggesting a topological insulator behavior for the material. This conclusion relied on the specific orientation of the materials with their respective axes aligned. In our study, we tested two additional configurations where the axes of Eu and InAs were oriented perpendicularly to each other. Using depth-resolved X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, we found that in these configurations, the energy levels of the valence bands for both materials overlap. This suggests that the observed band structure is sensitive to the boundary conditions at the interface of Eu and InAs.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we demonstrate that each class within this framework is effectively populated. Building upon this foundation, we develop a system of stages specifically for non-Borel sets in Baire space. This advancement allows us to derive an effective version of Laver's hierarchy of subsets of Baire space.

We develop a comprehensive framework by combining ordered semigroups and bounded distributive lattices to obtain ordered semilattices with a natural semiring structure. The integration of this framework with residuation principles yields bounded distributive residuated lattices, whose ordered semilattice components are naturally represented as squares of semilattices with specific semigroup structures. The work's key innovation is a novel approach to burdened algebraic structures, particularly a innovative method of extending bounded distributive residuated lattices, referred to as canonical extensions. This canonical extension technique establishes a full and exact embedding of a bounded distributive residuated lattice into an equivalent, completely regular one. Moreover, it is demonstrated that this property holds for broader categories such as ordered semilattice-expandable residuated lattices, semilattice-residuated lattices, and residuated lattices with a natural semiring structure. The study's implications extend to a wide range of algebraic structures, including semilattice-residuated mappings, semiring mapping sets, and the reconstruction of full and exact residuated lattices through specific morphism sets. The work's applications encompass the reconstruction of residuated lattices in the form of relation composition-based algebraic structures and the integration of fuzzy relation composition methods in the solution of the fuzzy declarative knowledge acquisition problem.

The mergers of compact binary systems consisting of black holes and neutron stars, including various combinations, can be observed through gravitational waves by observatories such as LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA. The merger events provide crucial information on the properties of their compact components, as well as their orbital motion. The merger signals can be analyzed to determine the change in orbital frequency, which is then fitted to a theoretical template. The template is created using general relativity equations that describe the orbital dynamics. The template is composed of multiple segments that correspond to different phases of the merger process. The segments are generated analytically and can be combined to form a continuous waveform. The LALSuite software can be used to generate the waveform. A new discovery has been made of NGTS-1b, a hot Jupiter orbiting around a star that has a similar metal content, which suggests a moderate level of metallicity. This discovery comes from a series of observations, including those from the NGTS-1 binary system, which also includes another planet that was discovered. The observations, including those from the Night Sky Telescope and other facilities, have led to a highly accurate measurement of the planet's size. Additionally, the data, combined with a series of observations over the course of a year, have provided a detailed model of the planet's atmosphere and its relationship with its star, which is consistent with other scientific findings. The overall density of the planet is found to be lower than previously estimated. As a result, a new model of the planet's internal structure has been developed, which indicates a core mass that is no greater than 15 Earth masses. The core of the planet is estimated to be about half the size of Earth.

A single agent decision making problem under restrictions is addressed, where operations need to be optimized under specific constraints on average handling and immediate responses, in accordance with constrained Markov decision processes. Operative instructions, determined at each time point, fall within predefined categories, analogous to their non-constrained counterparts, in order to comply with the constraints. This paper introduces a multi-phase approach to resolve such problems and presents two methods for its implementation, along with the assurance that optimal solutions exist and can be achieved through these methods. Furthermore, we establish a local convergence guarantee for one of the proposed methods and demonstrate its applicability to a concrete case of a single server queue with limitations, attaining a proven convergence guarantee in this context.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols, beginning with image segmentation. Despite hand-drawn images being prone to noise and incomplete, traditional pattern recognition techniques often struggle with segmentation. To address this challenge, a new approach is proposed, drawing from shape completion methods used in intelligent design systems. This approach employs a mathematical model that treats image formation as a form of deformation, incorporating noise and incomplete data. By applying this method to the completion task, a solution is found that minimizes the distance between consecutive shapes while adhering to the original image's features at the boundaries. This approach has been successfully applied to the recognition of handwritten mathematical equations created with the NxMath system, achieving accurate segmentation and pattern recognition using a combination of the proposed method and template matching.

A superconformal quantum mechanics derived from a supergravity background has its $Q$-cohomology represented by twisted Dolbeault cohomology classes on the complex submanifolds of the resolved space $\mathcal{X}$. As $Q$-cohomology is isomorphic to twisted holomorphic cohomology, it's argued that these BPS states correspond to twisted Dolbeault cohomology classes. By employing the Jones polynomial of a link, the twisted holomorphic cohomology and a specific link's twisted Dolbeault cohomology are computed, yielding an idea that the BPS index is represented by a polynomial of the Ka\breve{c}er-Vaksmann version of the Jones polynomial. Furthermore, it's shown that the twisted Dolbeault cohomology class for a link can be expressed as an integral of the Ka\bre{c}er-Vaksmann version of the Jones polynomial, for any resolved space $\mathcal{X}$.

We examine the role of network architecture in the dynamics of contagion processes, starting with homogeneous networks and incorporating random and small-world structures. Subsequently, we shift focus to heterogeneous networks, incorporating degree-corrected models, which reveal that structural heterogeneity can either exacerbate or mitigate the spread of contagions compared to homogeneous networks of equivalent size. Additionally, we investigate how this effect is influenced by the correlation between degrees of neighboring nodes, demonstrating that high heterogeneity can suppress contagion when degree correlations are present, and that the null model's accuracy predicts this behavior.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning techniques enjoy great popularity due to their ability to deliver practical solutions for a wide range of problems efficiently. Nevertheless, such methods can become trapped in a local optimum during action distribution exploration, hindering their effectiveness in achieving the best policy. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel integration of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and actor-critic reinforcement learning that facilitates efficient global exploration of the action space, yielding superior results compared to the traditional methods. Furthermore, we have designed a novel action buffer to mitigate overfitting and accelerate convergence. Experimental outcomes on six benchmark tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which consistently outperforms existing methods in terms of sample efficiency and final rewards.

It's common knowledge that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to 5 can be represented as either $6k \pm 1$ for a natural number $k$. In this paper, we demonstrate that such a representation is not unique by providing an alternative way to express prime numbers $p \geq 5$ using the form $12k \pm 1$, $6k \pm 1$, which is $12k \pm 1$, $\frac{6k \pm 1}{2} \pm 1$, respectively, where $k$ is a natural number. This approach simplifies the process of finding a prime number of the form $6k \pm 1$ by potentially checking a prime of the form $12k \pm 1$ first. The paper also discusses an algorithm that determines whether a given prime $p \geq 7$ is of the form $6k \pm 1$ or $12k \pm 1$ by utilizing a computationally efficient method that calculates the remainder of $p$ when divided by 12.

Autonomous navigation is a core challenge for many countries and a core topic in robotics research. However, current research often overlooks diverse real-world scenarios where sensors may fail due to environmental conditions like heat or cold. This research introduces several complex navigation scenarios with varying conditions and the extent of sensor limitations, and employs a few-shot learning approach using deep learning-based metric conditions and sensor failure metrics. The study utilizes a well-established benchmark dataset to evaluate several multi-objective optimization metrics that determine sensor failure and environment conditions, and identifies novel dataset characteristics not previously explored in other datasets. The research demonstrates the potential of this approach to discover unique dataset characteristics and assess various real-world scenarios through a combination of few-shot learning and deep learning.

The origins of various spectra in the bodies of the outer solar system's moons and small bodies remain enigmatic. Our research centers around a newly discovered spectral feature - a strong absorption near 3.0 micrometers - which could help explain the diverse spectral landscape in these regions. By utilizing a combination of models of organic and nanophase oxide minerals, we found that an organic compound with a similar structure to n-alkanes and an nanophase titanium oxide with specific characteristics, are likely responsible for this new spectral trait. Our findings also indicate that a mixture of these two minerals can plausibly account for the range of spectral absorptions and strengths observed in several cryovolcanic objects, such as Enceladus and Jupiter's moon Io. This implies that organic and/or oxide minerals, specifically those with nanophase titanium oxide, are present in Encelado and Io, among other bodies in the outer solar system.

Consider the set of non-free cyclic right modules over this ring, denoted $\mathcal{M}_n(q)$. A point in the affine plane $\mathbb{F}_{\mathbb{F}(q)}^2$ is represented as $(b_1, b_2)$. A subset of modules $\mathcal{M}_n(q)$, denoted $\mathcal{M}_n(q)^{(\Lambda)}$, is defined as those modules where each has a linear combination of its generators equivalent to a free module of rank 1, with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathbb{F}(q)}$ that are distinct and belong to a subset $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{F}_{\mathbb{F}(q)}^2$. It is established that $|\mathcal{M}_n(q)^{(\Lambda)}| \leq 4|\Lambda|^{n-1}$. In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred within extensions of those models. This is proven by establishing a corresponding relationship within a different type of model. The proof leverages a property discovered in another journal by Fischer, showing that the information content in forcing extensions remains consistent in models with only certain types of reals.

A new pessimism-based approach is presented for learning dynamic treatment regimes in the online setting. The framework is set within a general context, including cases where only bounds are known on reward and action spaces. The developed approach allows us to establish linear regret and regret on regret regret bounds that hold almost surely under various conditions. The presented analysis also considers scenarios where actions and rewards are known at a time lag. These results contribute to Bayesian methods for online learning and have potential applications in different domains, such as lagged online learning and model selection with delayed feedback. The presented approach can also facilitate the development of further online learning algorithms with different characteristics. The results are further demonstrated with several examples, including cases with unknown and known action and reward spaces.
